english:
but do you recognize that one man is a musician and another unmusical?” “I do.” “Which is the intelligent and which the unintelligent?” “The musician, I presume, is the intelligent and the unmusical the unintelligent.” “And is he not good in the things in which he is intelligent and bad in the things in which he is unintelligent?” “Yes.” “And the same of the physician?” “The same.” “Do you think then, my friend, that any musician in the tuning of a lyre would want to overreach another musician in the tightening and relaxing of the strings or would claim and think fit to exceed or outdo him?” “I do not.” “But would the the unmusical man?” “Of necessity,” he said.

“And how about the medical man?

chinese:
在规定饮食的时候，他会想要超过另一个懂医术的人，或超过医术所规定的做法吗？”
“当然不会。”
“但他会想要超过不懂医术的人吗？”
“是的。”
“那么，请你考察各种知识与无知的情形：你认为，一个有知识的人，会选择做出或说出与另一个有知识的人不同或更多的东西，而不选择在同一行动中，恰好做出与同类相同的事吗？”
“嗯，在这样的事情上，”他说，“也许必定如此。”
“可无知的人，那没有知识的人呢？他岂不是既想超过有知识的人，也想超过没有知识的人？”
english: In prescribing food and drink would he want to outdo the medical man or the medical procedure?” “Surely not.” “But he would the unmedical man?” “Yes.” “Consider then with regard to all forms of knowledge and ignorance whether you think that anyone who knows would choose to do or say other or more than what another who knows would do or say, and not rather exactly what his like would do in the same action.” “Why, perhaps it must be so,” he said, “in such cases.” “But what of the ignorant man—of him who does not know? Would he not overreach or outdo equally the knower and the ignorant?”

chinese:
“也许是吧。”
“而有知识的人是智慧的？”
“就算是。”
“智慧的人是好的？”
“就算是。”
“那么，善好而智慧的人不会想要超过同类，只会想要超过不同类和相反的人。”
“看来是的。”他说。“可坏人和无知的人，既会想要超过同类，也会想要超过不同类？”
“看来如此。”
“而我们所说的不正义的人，色拉叙马霍斯，岂不是既想超过不同类，也想超过同类？你不是这样说的吗？”
“我是这样说的。”他回答。
english: “It may be.” “But the one who knows is wise?” “I’ll say so.” “And the wise is good?” “I’ll say so.” “Then he who is good and wise will not wish to overreach his like but his unlike and opposite.” “It seems so,” he said. “But the bad man and the ignoramus will overreach both like and unlike?” “So it appears.” “And does not our unjust man, Thrasymachus, overreach both unlike and like? Did you not say that?” “I did,” he replied.

chinese:
“而正义的人不想超过同类，只想超过不同类？”
“是的。”
“那么，正义的人类似智慧而善好的人，不正义的人类似坏人和无知的人。”
“似乎是这样。”
“而且，我们同意过，各人类似什么样的人，他自己也就是什么样的人。”
“是的，我们同意过。”
“这样一来，我们这里得出的结果就是，正义的人善好而智慧，不正义的人坏而无知。”
色拉叙马霍斯承认所有这些，
english:
“But the just man will not overreach his like but only his unlike?” “Yes.” “Then the just man is like the wise and good, and the unjust is like the bad and the ignoramus.” “It seems likely.” “But furthermore we agreed that such is each as that to which he is like.” “Yes, we did.” “Then the just man has turned out on our hands to be good and wise and the unjust man bad and ignorant.”

Thrasymachus made all these admissions

chinese:
可不像我现在叙述得这样轻松；他一再抗拒，十分不情愿，汗流得厉害——当时正是夏天。也就在那时，我看见了从前从没见过的事：色拉叙马霍斯脸红了。不过，等我们终于得出结论，认为正义是德性和智慧，不正义是恶德和无知，我便说：“好，这一点就算已经确立了。但我们还曾断言，不正义是强而有力的东西。色拉叙马霍斯，你不记得了吗？”
“记得，”他说，“不过，你现在说的这些，我也不同意，而且我有话回答，
english: not as I now lightly narrate them, but with much baulking and reluctance and prodigious sweating, it being summer, and it was then I beheld what I had never seen before—Thrasymachus blushing. But when we did reach our conclusion that justice is virtue and wisdom and injustice vice and ignorance, “Good,” said I, “let this be taken as established. But we were also affirming that injustice is a strong and potent thing. Don’t you remember, Thrasymachus?” “I remember,” he said; “but I don’t agree with what you are now saying either and I have an answer to it,

chinese:
可要是我试着说出来，我很清楚，你准会说我在发表长篇大论。所以，你要么让我想说多长就说多长，要么，如果你更喜欢提问，就继续问；我会像我们听老太婆讲故事那样，说‘好极了’，点头表示赞同，摇头表示不赞同。”
“不，不，”我说，“不要违背你自己的看法。”
“就为了让你高兴，我偏要这样，”他说，“因为你不让我畅所欲言。可你还想要什么呢？”
“我确实不再要什么了，”我说，“不过，如果你打算这么做，就这么做吧，我来提问。”
“那么，问下去吧。”
“那么，我问的就是这一点，和先前一样，好让我们的探究依次推进。
english:
but if I were to attempt to state it, I know very well that you would say that I was delivering a harangue. Either then allow me to speak at such length as I desire, or, if you prefer to ask questions, go on questioning and I, as we do for old wives telling their tales, will say ‘Very good’ and will nod assent and dissent.” “No, no,” said I, “not counter to your own belief.” “Yes, to please you,” he said, “since you don’t allow me freedom of speech. And yet what more do you want?” “Nothing, indeed,” said I; “but if this is what you propose to do, do it and I will ask the questions.” “Ask on, then.”

“This, then, is the question I ask, the same as before, so that our inquiry may proceed in sequence.

chinese: 不正义与正义相比，性质究竟如何？因为我想，我们先前说的是，不正义比正义更有力、更强大。但现在，”我说，“如果正义是智慧和德性，那么我想，不难表明，它也比不正义更强大，因为不正义是无知——如今谁都不可能看不出这一点。可是，我想考察的，不只是这样简单的一点。色拉叙马霍斯，我想用类似下面这样的方式来考察。你会说，一个城邦可能是不正义的，它会
english: What is the nature of injustice as compared with justice? For the statement made, I believe, was that injustice is a more potent and stronger thing than justice. But now,” I said, “if justice is wisdom and virtue, it will easily, I take it, be shown to be also a stronger thing than injustice, since injustice is ignorance—no one could now fail to recognize that—but what I want is not quite so simple as that. I wish, Thrasymachus, to consider it in some such fashion as this. A city, you would say, may be unjust and

chinese:
试图不正义地奴役其他城邦，把它们置于奴役之下，并让许多城邦始终臣服于自己。”
“当然，”他说，“最好的城邦主要就会这么做，也就是那个不正义最彻底的城邦。”
“我明白，”我说，“这就是你的看法。不过，我正在考察的是这一点：一个这样压倒别的城邦的城邦，能够不凭正义就拥有这种力量，还是必定得把正义也结合进来？”
english: try to enslave other cities unjustly, have them enslaved and hold many of them in subjection.” “Certainly,” he said; “and this is what the best state will chiefly do, the state whose injustice is most complete.” “I understand,” I said, “that this was your view. But the point that I am considering is this, whether the city that thus shows itself superior to another will have this power without justice or whether she must of necessity combine it with justice.”

chinese:
“如果你刚才说的成立，正义就是智慧，那就凭正义；如果像我说的那样，那就凭不正义。”他回答。
“妙极了，色拉叙马霍斯，”我说，“你不仅点头、摇头，还作出了出色的回答。”
“我正努力让你高兴呢。”他回答。
“你太好了。不过，再让我高兴一回，告诉我这一点：你认为，一个城邦、一支军队、一伙强盗、一群窃贼，或任何试图共同采取行动的团体，假如彼此做不正义的事，还能成就什么吗？”
english:
“If, ” he replied, “what you were just now saying holds good, that justice is wisdom, with justice; if it is as I said, with injustice.” “Admirable, Thrasymachus,” I said; “you not only nod assent and dissent, but give excellent answers.” “I am trying to please you,” he replied.

“Very kind of you. But please me in one thing more and tell me this: do you think that a city, an army, or bandits, or thieves, or any other group that attempted any action in common, could accomplish anything if they wronged one another?”

chinese:
“当然不能。”他说。“但如果他们不这样做，岂不是更有可能成事？”
“当然。”
“因为，色拉叙马霍斯，不正义带来的是派系争斗、仇恨和自相残杀的冲突，正义带来的却是同心和友爱。不是这样吗？”
“就算是吧，”他回答，“我不和你争。”
“朋友，你真好。不过，请告诉我：如果不正义的作用，就是无论在哪里出现都滋生仇恨，那么，它在自由人或奴隶之间发生时，岂不会使他们彼此仇恨、互相争斗，无法有效地共同行动？”
english: “Certainly not,” said he. “But if they didn’t, wouldn’t they be more likely to?” “Assuredly.” “For factions, Thrasymachus, are the outcome of injustice, and hatreds and internecine conflicts, but justice brings oneness of mind and love. Is it not so?” “So be it,” he replied, “not to differ from you.” “That is good of you, my friend; but tell me this: if it is the business of injustice to engender hatred wherever it is found, will it not, when it springs up either among freemen or slaves, cause them to hate and be at strife with one another, and make them incapable of effective action in common?”

chinese:
“当然会。”
“那么，假如它发生在两个人之间，他们岂不会彼此不和、相互仇恨，既成为对方的敌人，又成为正义的人的敌人？”
“会的。”他说。“那么，假如不正义发生在一个人之内，你会告诉我，它就失去了自己的力量和作用，还是依然保有它们？”
“就算依然保有吧。”他说。“而它的力量岂不是已经很清楚了：无论它出现于城邦、家庭、军营，还是别的任何东西之中，
english:
“By all means.” “Suppose, then, it springs up between two, will they not be at outs with and hate each other and be enemies both to one another and to the just?” “They will,” he said. “And then will you tell me that if injustice arises in one it will lose its force and function or will it none the less keep it?” “Have it that it keeps it,” he said.

“And is it not apparent that its force is such that wherever it is found in city, family, camp, or in anything else

chinese:
首先都会由于派系争斗和分歧，使那个东西无法与自身协调行动；其次，又会使它成为自身的敌人，并且无论在什么情形下，都与它的对立面——正义者——为敌。不是这样吗？”
“当然。”
“那么，我想，它出现在个人之内，也会产生它本性所能产生的这一切效果。首先，它会由于内在的争斗和自身的不一致，使他不能成就任何事；其次，会使他成为自己的敌人，也成为正义的人的敌人。不是这样吗？”
“是的。”
“不过，朋友，诸神也是正义的。”
english: it first renders the thing incapable of cooperation with itself owing to faction and difference, and secondly an enemy to itself and to its opposite in every case, the just? Isn’t that so?” “By all means.” “Then in the individual too, I presume, its presence will operate all these effects which it is its nature to produce. It will in the first place make him incapable of accomplishing anything because of inner faction and lack of self-agreement, and then an enemy to himself and to the just. Is it not so?” “Yes.” “But, my friend, the gods too are just.”

chinese:
“就算他们是吧。”他说。“那么看来，不正义的人也会被诸神厌恶，正义的人则为诸神所喜爱。”
“你放心享用你的这席话吧，”他说，“我不会反对你，免得得罪你在这里的那些拥护者。”
“那么，请继续像刚才一样回答，”我说，“把我这顿宴席摆足，为我补全。如今我们看到，正义的人更有智慧、更好，也更有行动能力，而不正义的人无法采取任何共同的行动；
english: “Have it that they are,” he said. “So to the gods also, it seems, the unjust man will be hateful, but the just man dear.” “Revel in your discourse,” he said, “without fear, for I shall not oppose you, so as not to offend your partisans here.” “Fill up the measure of my feast, then, and complete it for me,” I said, “by continuing to answer as you have been doing. Now that the just appear to be wiser and better and more capable of action and the unjust incapable of any common action,

chinese: 我们还看到，如果我们说，某些不正义的人曾经有力地联合起来办成一件事，这话并不完全真实。因为，要是他们彻底不正义，就不会不向彼此下手。显然，他们身上还存有某种正义，使他们在对付所攻击的人的同时，不至于也对彼此做不正义的事。他们正是凭借这一点，才办成了所做的事；他们出去做不正义的事时，只被不正义败坏了一半，因为那些完全不正义、坏透了的恶棍，
english: and that if we ever say that any men who are unjust have vigorously combined to put something over, our statement is not altogether true, for they would not have kept their hands from one another if they had been thoroughly unjust, but it is obvious that there was in them some justice which prevented them from wronging at the same time one another too as well as those whom they attacked; and by dint of this they accomplished whatever they did and set out to do injustice only half corrupted by injustice, since utter rascals completely unjust

chinese:
完全没有有效行动的能力——我认为，这一切才是真实的，而不是你起初提出的主张。不过，正义的人是否也比不正义的人生活得更好、更幸福，也就是我们后来提出要考察的问题，现在还得考察。我想，即使就已经说过的话来看，似乎也已经是这样了。尽管如此，我们仍须更仔细地检验。因为我们讨论的不是寻常小事，而是人应当怎样生活。”
“继续你的探究吧。”他说。“我继续，”我说，“那么，请告诉我，你会不会说，
english: are completely incapable of effective action—all this I understand to be the truth, and not what you originally laid down. But whether it is also true that the just have a better life than the unjust and are happier, which is the question we afterwards proposed for examination, is what we now have to consider. It appears even now that they are, I think, from what has already been said. But all the same we must examine it more carefully. For it is no ordinary matter that we are discussing, but the right conduct of life.” “Proceed with your inquiry,” he said. “I proceed,” said I. “Tell me then—would you say

chinese:
马有一种特有的工作或功能？”
“我会。”
“你愿不愿意把马或任何其他东西的工作界定为：只有借助它才能做到，或者借助它能做得最好的事？”
“我不明白。”他回答。“好，换个说法：除了眼睛，你还能用别的什么来看吗？”
“当然不能。”
“再说，除了耳朵，你还能用别的什么来听吗？”
“绝不能。”
“你说这些分别是这两个器官的功能，岂不是说得对？”
“当然。”
“再举一个例子，
english:
that a horse has a specific work or function?” “I would.” “Would you be willing to define the work of a horse or of anything else to be that which one can do only with it or best with it?” “I don’t understand,” he replied. “Well, take it this way: is there anything else with which you can see except the eyes?” “Certainly not.” “Again, could you hear with anything but ears?” “By no means.” “Would you not rightly say that these are the functions of these (organs)?” “By all means.”

“Once more,

chinese:
你可以用短剑、小刀以及许多别的工具来修剪葡萄藤的枝条。”
“当然。”
“但我想，都比不上专为这个目的打造的修枝刀。”
“这是真的。”
“那么，我们岂不是必须把这件事看作它的工作或功能？”
“必须。”
“那么我想，你现在更能明白我刚才那个问题的意思了：一件东西的工作，岂不就是只有它能完成，或它比其他一切东西完成得更好的事？”
“嗯，”他说，“我明白了，也同意一件东西的工作就是如此。”
english:
you could use a dirk to trim vine branches and a knife and many other instruments.” “Certainly.” “But nothing so well, I take it, as a pruning-knife fashioned for this purpose.” “That is true.” “Must we not then assume this to be the work or function of that?” “We must.”

“You will now, then, I fancy, better apprehend the meaning of my question when I asked whether that is not the work of a thing which it only or it better than anything else can perform.” “Well,” he said, “I do understand, and agree that the work of anything is that.”

chinese:
“很好，”我说，“凡是具有特定工作或功能的东西，你不也认为，它具有自己特有的德性或优良能力吗？我们回到同样的例子。我们说眼睛有一种功能？”
“有。”
“眼睛也有一种德性吗？”
“有。”
“耳朵不是也有一种功能吗？”
“是的。”
“那么也有一种德性？”
“也有。”
“其他一切东西呢？情况不也是一样吗？”
“一样。”
“现在请留意：眼睛能不能很好地完成它的功能，
english: “Very good,” said I. “Do you not also think that there is a specific virtue or excellence of everything for which a specific work or function is appointed? Let us return to the same examples. The eyes we say have a function?” “They have.” “Is there also a virtue of the eyes?” “There is.” “And was there not a function of the ears?” “Yes.” “And so also a virtue?” “Also a virtue.” “And what of all other things? Is the case not the same?” “The same.” “Take note now. Could the eyes possibly fulfil their function well

chinese:
如果它缺少自己固有的优良能力，反而具有相应的缺陷？”
“怎么可能呢？”他说，“因为我想，你指的是失明代替了视力。”
“无论那种优良能力是什么，”我说，“我还没有问到这一点。我只是在问：凡是起作用的东西，是否都凭借自己的德性把自己的工作做好，而由于自己的缺陷把工作做坏？”
“这一点，”他说，“你可以肯定是真的。”
“那么，耳朵也是如此：如果失去自身的德性，就会把它的工作做坏？”
“当然。”
“那么，我们也把同一道理用于一切东西吗？”
english: if they lacked their own proper excellence and had in its stead the defect?” “How could they?” he said; “for I presume you meant blindness instead of vision.” “Whatever,” said I, “the excellence may be. For I have not yet come to that question, but am only asking whether whatever operates will not do its own work well by its own virtue and badly by its own defect.” “That much,” he said, “you may affirm to be true.” “Then the ears, too, if deprived of their own virtue will do their work ill?” “Assuredly.” “And do we then apply the same principle to all things?”

chinese:
“我想是的。”
“那么，接着考察这一点。灵魂有没有一种工作，是你用世上任何别的东西都无法完成的？例如管理、统治、思虑，以及诸如此类的事，除了灵魂，你还能恰当地把这些归给别的什么，说是它特有的工作吗？”
“不能归给别的东西。”
“再说，活着呢？我们也说这是灵魂的功能吗？”
“当然。”他说。“我们不是也说，灵魂有一种优良能力，也就是德性吗？”
english: “I think so.” “Then next consider this. The soul, has it a work which you couldn’t accomplish with anything else in the world, as for example, management, rule, deliberation, and the like, is there anything else than soul to which you could rightly assign these and say that they were its peculiar work?” “Nothing else.” “And again life? Shall we say that too is the function of the soul?” “Most certainly,” he said. “And do we not also say that there is an excellence virtue of the soul?”

chinese:
“是的。”
“灵魂若失去自己的德性，还能把自己的工作做好吗，还是绝不可能？”
“绝不可能。”
“那么必然地，坏的灵魂会把统治和管理做坏，好的灵魂则会在所有这些事情上做好。”
“必然如此。”
“我们不是同意过，灵魂的优良能力或德性是正义，它的缺陷是不正义吗？”
“是的，我们同意过。”
“那么，正义的灵魂和正义的人就会生活得好，不正义的则生活得坏？”
“照你的推理，”他说，“看来如此。”
english: “We do.” “Will the soul ever accomplish its own work well if deprived of its own virtue, or is this impossible?” “It is impossible.” “Of necessity, then, a bad soul will govern and manage things badly while the good soul will in all these things do well. ” “Of necessity.” “And did we not agree that the excellence or virtue of soul is justice and its defect injustice?” “Yes, we did.” “The just soul and the just man then will live well and the unjust ill?” “So it appears,” he said, “by your reasoning.”

chinese:
“而且，生活得好的人有福而幸福，生活得不好的人则恰好相反。”
“当然。”
“那么，正义的人幸福，不正义的人不幸。”
“就算是吧。”他说。“但不幸当然无利可言，有利的是幸福。”
“不幸当然无利。”
“那么，最可敬的色拉叙马霍斯，不正义绝不可能比正义更有益。”
“苏格拉底，就让这话为你在本狄斯节上的宴席收尾吧。”
“色拉叙马霍斯，这顿宴席是你供给的，”我说，“因为你现在对我温和了，不再生气。不过，我吃得并不好，
english: “But furthermore, he who lives well is blessed and happy, and he who does not the contrary.” “Of course.” “Then the just is happy and the unjust miserable.” “So be it,” he said. “But it surely does not pay to be miserable, but to be happy.” “Of course not.” “Never, then, most worshipful Thrasymachus, can injustice be more profitable than justice.” “Let this complete your entertainment, Socrates, at the festival of Bendis.” “A feast furnished by you, Thrasymachus,” I said, “now that you have become gentle with me and are no longer angry. I have not dined well, however—

chinese: 这是我自己的过错，不是你的过错。就像贪吃的人，每逢一道菜从面前传过，就抓来尝一口，还没来得及好好享用前一道，我想我也是这样：还没找到我们最初探究的对象——正义是什么——就把它放下，转而考察有关它的另一件事，即它究竟是恶德和无知，还是智慧和德性。后来，又突然冒出了一个主张，说不正义比正义更有益，我又忍不住从前一个题目转向了这一个。所以，对我来说，
english: by my own fault, not yours. But just as gluttons snatch at every dish that is handed along and taste it before they have properly enjoyed the preceding, so I, methinks, before finding the first object of our inquiry—what justice is—let go of that and set out to consider something about it, namely whether it is vice and ignorance or wisdom and virtue; and again, when later the view was sprung upon us that injustice is more profitable than justice I could not refrain from turning to that from the other topic. So that for me

chinese: 眼下这场讨论的结果，就是我一无所知。因为，如果我不知道正义是什么，我就很难知道它是不是一种德性，也很难知道拥有它的人究竟幸福不幸福。”
english: the present outcome of the discussion is that I know nothing. For if I don’t know what the just is, I shall hardly know whether it is a virtue or not, and whether its possessor is or is not happy.”

chinese:
苏格拉底
我说完这些话，本以为这个问题已经谈完，结果却发现，这一切不过是个序曲。格劳孔做什么事向来都无所畏惧，敢于进取；这一次，他也不肯就这样接受色拉叙马霍斯放弃自己的主张。他说：“苏格拉底，你想让我们看起来被你说服，
english: When I had said this I supposed that I was done with the subject, but it all turned out to be only a prelude. For Glaucon, who is always an intrepid enterprising spirit in everything, would not on this occasion acquiesce in Thrasymachus’s abandonment of his case, but said, “Socrates, is it your desire to seem to have persuaded us

chinese:
还是真正说服我们：正义在一切情况下都比不正义好？”
“如果由我选择，”我说，“当然是真正说服你们。”
“那么，你还没有做到自己想做的事。请告诉我：你是否承认，有一类好东西，我们愿意拥有它，不是因为渴望它随后带来的结果，而是因为它本身就值得欢迎？例如欢乐，以及那些无害的快乐；除了享有并保持这种愉悦，它们后来并不产生别的结果。”
english: or really to persuade us that it is without exception better to be just than unjust?” “Really,” I said, “if the choice rested with me.” “Well, then, you are not doing what you wish. For tell me: do you agree that there is a kind of good which we would choose to possess, not from desire for its after effects, but welcoming it for its own sake? As, for example, joy and such pleasures are harmless and nothing results from them afterwards save to have and to hold the enjoyment.”

chinese:
“我承认有这一类。”我说。
“是不是还有一类，我们既为它本身，也为它的结果而喜爱它，例如理解力、视力和健康？我想，我们欢迎这些东西，是出于这两方面的理由。”
“是的。”我说。
“你能不能再辨认出第三类好东西？身体锻炼、生病时接受治疗、医治的技艺，以及一般的谋利活动，都属于这一类。我们会说，它们虽辛苦而令人不快，却有益处；就它们本身而言，
english: “I recognise that kind,” said I. “And again a kind that we love both for its own sake and for its consequences, such as understanding, sight, and health? For these presume we welcome for both reasons.” “Yes,” I said. “And can you discern a third form of good under which falls exercise and being healed when sick and the art of healing and the making of money generally? For of them we would say that they are laborious and painful yet beneficial, and for their own sake

chinese:
我们并不愿意接受，只是为了它们带来的报酬和其他好处，才去接受。”
“当然，”我说，“我也得承认这第三类。不过，这又怎样呢？”
“你把正义放在哪一类里？”他问。
english: we would not accept them, but only for the rewards and other benefits that accrue from them.” “Why yes,” I said, “I must admit this third class also. But what of it?” “In which of these classes do you place justice?” he said.

chinese:
“依我看，”我说，“它属于最美好的一类：一个人若要幸福，就必须既为它本身，也为它的结果而喜爱它。”
“可是大多数人并不这样想，”他说，“他们认为，正义属于辛苦的那一类：人必须为了报酬和世人评价所带来的名声而实行它；至于它本身，则该像一种苦难那样避开。”
“我知道，”我说，“这正是一般人的看法。色拉叙马霍斯刚才也一直把正义当成这样的东西加以贬低，同时赞扬不正义。只是看来，我学得有些迟钝。”
“那么，”
english:
“In my opinion,” I said, “it belongs in the fairest class, that which a man who is to be happy must love both for its own sake and for the results.” “Yet the multitude,” he said, “do not think so, but that it belongs to the toilsome class of things that must be practised for the sake of rewards and repute due to opinion but that in itself is to be shunned as an affliction.”

“I am aware,” said I, “that that is the general opinion and Thrasymachus has for some time been disparaging it as such and praising injustice. But I, it seems, am somewhat slow to learn.” “Come now,”

chinese: 他说，“也听听我的话，看看你同不同意。在我看来，色拉叙马霍斯向你让步得太早，仿佛一条被你的笛声迷住的蛇。但关于正义和不正义，刚才提出的证明，还不能使我满意。我想听的是：它们各自究竟是什么，以及它们住在灵魂之中，单凭自身各有什么力量、产生什么作用；至于它们带来的报酬和后果，我想先撇开。因此，如果你赞成，我打算这样做：我要重新提出
english: he said, “hear what I too have to say and see if you agree with me. For Thrasymachus seems to me to have given up to you too soon, as if he were a serpent that you had charmed, but I am not yet satisfied with the proof that has been offered about justice and injustice. For what I desire is to hear what each of them is and what potency and effect it has in and of itself dwelling in the soul, but to dismiss their rewards and consequences. This, then, is what I propose to do, with your concurrence. I will renew

chinese: 色拉叙马霍斯的论证，首先说明人们怎样解释正义的本性和起源；其次，说明所有实行正义的人都出于不情愿，把它看成不得不做的事，而非一种好东西；第三，说明他们这样做有似乎说得通的理由，因为据他们说，不正义者的生活确实远比正义者好。苏格拉底，我自己并不相信这些话；但色拉叙马霍斯和无数其他人的论调在耳边不断轰响，使我困惑。至于为正义辩护、
english: the argument of Thrasymachus and will first state what men say is the nature and origin of justice; secondly, that all who practise it do so reluctantly, regarding it as something necessary and not as a good; and thirdly, that they have plausible grounds for thus acting, since forsooth the life of the unjust man is far better than that of the just man—as they say; though I, Socrates, don’t believe it. Yet I am disconcerted when my ears are dinned by the arguments of Thrasymachus and innumerable others. But the case for justice,

chinese:
证明正义胜过不正义的论述，我从未听到有人按照我所希望的方式讲出来。我想听的，是单就正义本身而作的赞颂；而我认为，最有可能让我听到这种话的人就是你。所以，我将尽力赞扬不正义的生活，用这样的说法示范：我希望你随后怎样贬斥不正义、赞扬正义。请考虑一下，我这个提议是否合你的心意。”
“再没有什么比这更合我的心意了。”我说，
english: to prove that it is better than injustice, I have never yet heard stated by any as I desire to hear it. What I desire is to hear an encomium on justice in and by itself. And I think I am most likely to get that from you. For which reason I will lay myself out in praise of the life of injustice, and in so speaking will give you an example of the manner in which I desire to hear from you in turn the dispraise of injustice and the praise of justice. Consider whether my proposal pleases you.” “Nothing could please me more,” said I;

chinese:
“一个有头脑的人，还会更乐于反复谈论、反复听取什么别的话题呢？”
“太好了，”他说，“现在请听我说过的第一个问题：正义的本性和起源。人们说，按照自然，做不正义的事是好事，遭受不正义则是坏事；不过，受不正义之害的坏处，超过了行不正义所得的好处。因此，人们相互作恶，又相互受害，两种滋味都尝过之后，那些没有力量
english:
“for on what subject would a man of sense rather delight to hold and hear discourse again and again?” “That is excellent,” he said; “and now listen to what I said would be the first topic—the nature and origin of justice.”

By nature, they say, to commit injustice is a good and to suffer it is an evil, but that the excess of evil in being wronged is greater than the excess of good in doing wrong. So that when men do wrong and are wronged by one another and taste of both, those who lack the power

chinese: 避开受害、同时取得作恶之利的人，便认为，彼此订立契约，既不做不正义的事，也不遭受不正义，对自己是有利的。他们说，这就是人与人之间立法和订约的开端；法律所命令的，人们称为合法和正义。这就是正义的起源及其本质：它是最好与最坏之间的折中。最好的是作恶而不受惩罚，最坏的是遭到侵害却无力报复。他们告诉我们，正义处在这两者之间，所以受到接受和赞许，
english: to avoid the one and take the other determine that it is for their profit to make a compact with one another neither to commit nor to suffer injustice; and that this is the beginning of legislation and covenants between men, and that they name the commandment of the law the lawful and the just, and that this is the genesis and essential nature of justice—a compromise between the best, which is to do wrong with impunity, and the worst, which is to be wronged and be impotent to get one’s revenge. Justice, they tell us, being mid-way between the two, is accepted and approved,

chinese:
并不是因为它是真正的好东西，而是因为人们缺乏行不正义的力量，才尊重它。任何有力量作恶、又真正算得上一个“男子汉”的人，都绝不会同别人约定既不害人也不受害；否则他就是疯了。苏格拉底，按照这种说法，正义的本性就是如此，它就是在这样的条件下产生的。
“至于第二点，即实行正义的人并非出于自愿，而是因为没有力量实行不正义，我们若在思想中作如下设想，大概最容易看清：
english:
not as a real good, but as a thing honored in the lack of vigor to do injustice, since anyone who had the power to do it and was in reality ‘a man’ would never make a compact with anybody either to wrong nor to be wronged; for he would be mad. The nature, then, of justice is this and such as this, Socrates, and such are the conditions in which it originates, according to the theory.

But as for the second point, that those who practise it do so unwillingly and from want of power to commit injustice—we shall be most likely to apprehend that if we entertain some such supposition as this in thought:

chinese: 让正义者和不正义者都获得随心所欲的自由和力量，然后在想象中跟着他们，看看各自的欲望会把他们带向哪里。这样，我们就会当场发现，正义者也在采取同不正义者一样的行动，因为他也要为自己争取更多利益。每一种生物都天生把这种利益当成好东西来追求，只是法律的约定强行把它扭转过来，使它尊重“平等”。我所说的自由，最接近于这样一种情形：假定他们拥有那种力量，
english: if we grant to each, the just and the unjust, licence and power to do whatever he pleases, and then accompany them in imagination and see whither his desire will conduct each. We should then catch the just man in the very act of resorting to the same conduct as the unjust man because of the self-advantage which every creature by its nature pursues as a good, while by the convention of law it is forcibly diverted to paying honor to ‘equality.’ The licence that I mean would be most nearly such as would result from supposing them to have the power

chinese: 也就是传说中吕底亚人古格斯的祖先曾得到的力量。据说，他是当时吕底亚统治者手下的牧羊人。一场暴雨和一次地震之后，他放牧的地方大地裂开，出现了一道深渊。他看见后十分惊奇，便下到深渊里。传说他在那里看见了种种奇观，其中有一匹中空的铜马，马身上开着小门。他探头向里面看去，看见一具尸体，身躯似乎比凡人更为高大，
english: which men say once came to the ancestor of Gyges the Lydian. They relate that he was a shepherd in the service of the ruler at that time of Lydia, and that after a great deluge of rain and an earthquake the ground opened and a chasm appeared in the place where he was pasturing; and they say that he saw and wondered and went down into the chasm; and the story goes that he beheld other marvels there and a hollow bronze horse with little doors, and that he peeped in and saw a corpse within, as it seemed, of more than mortal stature,

chinese: 身上别无他物，只有手上戴着一枚金戒指。他把戒指取下来，便出了深渊。后来，牧人们依照惯例聚会，每月向国王报告羊群的情况，他也戴着戒指参加。他坐在那里时，偶然把戒指的镶座转向自己，也就是转向手掌内侧。据说，这样一来，他在身旁那些人的眼中便隐去了形体，
english:
and that there was nothing else but a gold ring on its hand, which he took off and went forth. And when the shepherds held their customary assembly to make their monthly report to the king about the flocks, he also attended wearing the ring.”

So as he sat there it chanced that he turned the collet of the ring towards himself, towards the inner part of his hand, and when this took place they say that he became invisible

chinese: 他们谈论他，仿佛他不在场一样。他十分惊讶，又摸弄戒指，把镶座转向外侧，于是重新显露出来。注意到这一点之后，他试验戒指是否真有这种功效，发现只要把镶座转向内侧，他就隐身；转向外侧，他就现身。他明白这一点，立刻设法使自己成为前往国王那里的使者之一。
english: to those who sat by him and they spoke of him as absent and that he was amazed, and again fumbling with the ring turned the collet outwards and so became visible. On noting this he experimented with the ring to see if it possessed this virtue, and he found the result to be that when he turned the collet inwards he became invisible, and when outwards visible; and becoming aware of this, he immediately managed things so that he became one of the messengers

chinese: 到了那里，他勾引了王后，又在她的帮助下袭击国王，把他杀死，夺取了他的王国。现在，假若有两枚这样的戒指，正义者戴上一枚，不正义者戴上另一枚，看来就找不到一个意志坚硬如金刚的人，还肯坚持正义，克制自己的双手，不去碰别人的财物。因为他可以随心所欲，甚至在市场上拿走自己想要的东西而不受惩罚，
english: who went up to the king, and on coming there he seduced the king’s wife and with her aid set upon the king and slew him and possessed his kingdom. If now there should be two such rings, and the just man should put on one and the unjust the other, no one could be found, it would seem, of such adamantine temper as to persevere in justice and endure to refrain his hands from the possessions of others and not touch them, though he might with impunity take what he wished even from the marketplace,

chinese: 可以进入别人家里，和自己喜欢的人同床，可以杀死任何想杀的人，解开任何想释放之人的锁链；在所有其他事情上，也可以在人间像神一样行事。这样做的时候，他同另一个人的行为毫无区别，两个人都会走上同一条道路。有人会说，这就充分证明：没有人自愿正义，人们只是被迫如此，因为他们相信正义并非自己的好处；任何人只要以为自己有力量作恶，就会作恶。
english: and enter into houses and lie with whom he pleased, and slay and loose from bonds whomsoever he would, and in all other things conduct himself among mankind as the equal of a god. And in so acting he would do no differently from the other man, but both would pursue the same course. And yet this is a great proof, one might argue, that no one is just of his own will but only from constraint, in the belief that justice is not his personal good, inasmuch as every man, when he supposes himself to have the power to do wrong, does wrong.

chinese: 因为每个人都相信，不正义给他个人带来的利益远远多于正义；而提出这种理论的人还会坚持，他们相信的是实情。一个人若已经掌握了这样的自由，却拒绝作任何恶事，也不肯伸手拿别人的财物，那么，所有注意到他的人，都会认为他最可怜，是个十足的傻瓜。不过，在彼此面前，他们仍会赞扬他，相互欺骗，因为他们都害怕自己遭受不正义。这一点就说到这里。
english: For that there is far more profit for him personally in injustice than in justice is what every man believes, and believes truly, as the proponent of this theory will maintain. For if anyone who had got such a licence within his grasp should refuse to do any wrong or lay his hands on others’ possessions, he would be regarded as most pitiable and a great fool by all who took note of it, though they would praise him before one another’s faces, deceiving one another because of their fear of suffering injustice. So much for this point.

chinese: “现在，我们来裁决这两种生活。只有把最彻底的正义者和最彻底的不正义者分开，我们才能作出正确判断；不这样做，就不能。那么，该怎样把他们分开呢？办法如下：我们不能从不正义者那里减去丝毫不正义，也不能从正义者那里减去丝毫正义，而要假定两人在各自的行为方式上都达到了完满。首先，不正义者必须像高明的工匠一样行事。例如，一流的舵手或医生，能够觉察自己技艺中可能做到与不可能做到的事情之间的区别，
english:
But to come now to the decision between our two kinds of life, if we separate the most completely just and the most completely unjust man, we shall be able to decide rightly, but if not, not. How, then, is this separation to be made? Thus: we must subtract nothing of his injustice from the unjust man or of his justice from the just, but assume the perfection of each in his own mode of conduct.”

In the first place, the unjust man must act as clever craftsmen do: a first-rate pilot or physician, for example, feels the difference between impossibilities and possibilities in his art

chinese: 尝试前者，放弃后者；而且，即使偶然失手，也有能力纠正自己的错误。同样，一个以恰当方式行不正义的人，若要成为彻底的不正义者，我们就必须假定他能逃过侦查；被抓住的人，只能算笨拙的生手。因为不正义的顶点，就是实际不正义却显得正义。因此，对完全不正义的人，我们必须赋予完全的不正义，一点也不能扣除；我们必须让他在犯下最大的恶行时，仍为自己赢得最正义的名声；
english: and attempts the one and lets the others go; and then, too, if he does happen to trip, he is equal to correcting his error. Similarly, the unjust man who attempts injustice rightly must be supposed to escape detection if he is to be altogether unjust, and we must regard the man who is caught as a bungler. For the height of injustice is to seem just without being so. To the perfectly unjust man, then, we must assign perfect injustice and withhold nothing of it, but we must allow him, while committing the greatest wrongs, to have secured for himself the greatest reputation for justice;

chinese: 即使偶然失手，也必须承认他有纠正错误的力量：如果有哪件恶行暴露，他能凭借善于说服人的口才脱身；需要武力时，他又能凭借勇气、力量，以及朋友和钱财的储备，使用武力。我们树立起这样一个不正义者之后，还必须在论述中把正义者放在他身旁：一个质朴而高尚的人，用埃斯库罗斯的话说，他不愿显得好，而愿真正是好人。然后，我们必须剥去他的表象。因为，如果他被认为正义，
english: and if he does happen to trip, we must concede to him the power to correct his mistakes by his ability to speak persuasively if any of his misdeeds come to light, and when force is needed, to employ force by reason of his manly spirit and vigor and his provision of friends and money; and when we have set up an unjust man of this character, our theory must set the just man at his side—a simple and noble man, who, in the phrase of Aeschylus, does not wish to seem but be good. Then we must deprive him of the seeming. For if he is going to be thought just

chinese: 他就会因为这种评价而得到荣誉和礼物。这样，我们便无法确定，他是为了正义本身而正义，还是为了礼物和荣誉。因此，除了正义，我们必须把他所有的一切都剥去，使他的处境同我们所设想的另一个人完全相反。他虽然没有做过任何错事，却必须背负最不正义的名声，好让他的正义受到考验，看他会不会因为恶名及其后果而动摇。但要让他始终坚持自己的道路，直到死亡，
english: he will have honors and gifts because of that esteem. We cannot be sure in that case whether he is just for justice’s sake or for the sake of the gifts and the honors. So we must strip him bare of everything but justice and make his state the opposite of his imagined counterpart. Though doing no wrong he must have the repute of the greatest injustice, so that he may be put to the test as regards justice through not softening because of ill repute and the consequences thereof. But let him hold on his course unchangeable even unto death,

chinese:
一生显得不正义，实际却是正义的。这样，两个人分别达到不正义和正义的极点，我们便可以判断，他们之中哪一个更幸福。”
“我的天，亲爱的格劳孔，”我说，“你把这两个人打磨得多么用力，简直像打磨雕像，好让他们登场竞逐奖赏。”
“我尽了自己的能力。”他回答，“如果两个人的本性就是这样，那么，我想，要讲清等待各人的将是什么生活，就容易了。
english:
seeming all his life to be unjust though being just, that so, both men attaining to the limit, the one of injustice, the other of justice, we may pass judgement which of the two is the happier.”

“Bless me, my dear Glaucon,” said I, “how strenuously you polish off each of your two men for the competition for the prize as if it were a statue.” “To the best of my ability,” he replied, “and if such is the nature of the two, it becomes an easy matter, I fancy, to unfold the tale of the sort of life that awaits each.

chinese: 所以，我们必须把它讲出来。苏格拉底，即使我的措辞有些粗暴残酷，你也不要以为是我自己这样说；这是那些把不正义看得高于正义的人所说的话。他们会说：这样一个正义者，将受到鞭打、拷问和锁链的折磨，
english:
We must tell it, then; and even if my language is somewhat rude and brutal, you must not suppose, Socrates, that it is I who speak thus, but those who commend injustice above justice.”

What they will say is this: that such being his disposition the just man will have to endure the lash, the rack, chains,

chinese:
双眼被烙铁灼伤，最后，在受尽各种酷刑之后，被钉在刑架上。他这才学会一个教训：我们应该渴望的，不是真正正义，而是显得正义。这样看来，埃斯库罗斯的那句话用在不正义者身上，反倒贴切得多。他们会说，不正义者追求紧贴实际、紧贴真实的东西，不依照世人的评价安排生活，因此，他确实不是想显得不正义，而是想真正不正义：
‘耕耘自己才智的深沟，
从中长出精明谋略的果实。’
（埃斯库罗斯《七将攻忒拜》592–594 行）
english:
the branding-iron in his eyes, and finally, after every extremity of suffering, he will be crucified, and so will learn his lesson that not to be but to seem just is what we ought to desire. And the saying of Aeschylus was, it seems, far more correctly applicable to the unjust man. For it is literally true, they will say, that the unjust man, as pursuing what clings closely to reality, to truth, and not regulating his life by opinion, desires not to seem but to be unjust,‘
Exploiting the deep furrows of his wit ’ ‘
From which there grows the fruit of counsels shrewd,’

chinese: 首先，他凭借正义的名声，在城邦中担任官职、掌握统治权；其次，他可以从自己选择的任何家族娶妻，把儿女嫁娶给任何中意的人，和任何愿意交往的人交易、合作。在所有这些事务中，他都为自己取得优势和利益，因为他对实行不正义毫不忌惮。因此，他们说，不论他卷入公诉还是私讼，都能胜诉，压倒对手；占了上风，他便致富，帮助朋友，伤害敌人；
english: first office and rule in the state because of his reputation for justice, then a wife from any family he chooses, and the giving of his children in marriage to whomsoever he pleases, dealings and partnerships with whom he will, and in all these transactions advantage and profit for himself because he has no squeamishness about committing injustice; and so they say that if he enters into lawsuits, public or private, he wins and gets the better of his opponents, and, getting the better, is rich and benefits his friends and harms his enemies;

chinese:
他献上充足而壮丽的祭品和供物敬奉诸神，对自己喜欢的人以及诸神，他也比正义者侍奉得周到，讨好得殷勤。因此，他完全可以合理地期待，上天的眷顾也会更多地落在他身上，而非正义者身上。苏格拉底，他们说，神和人为不正义者预备的生活，比等待正义者的生活要好上这么多。”
格劳孔说完这些话，我正想
english:
and he performs sacrifices and dedicates votive offerings to the gods adequately and magnificently, and he serves and pays court to men whom he favors and to the gods far better than the just man, so that he may reasonably expect the favor of heaven also to fall rather to him than to the just. So much better they say, Socrates, is the life that is prepared for the unjust man from gods and men than that which awaits the just.”

When Glaucon had thus spoken, I had a mind

chinese:
作些回答，他的兄弟阿德曼托斯却说：“苏格拉底，你不会以为，这个问题已经说全了吧？”
“怎么，还有什么？”我问。
“最要紧的一点，”他说，“还没有提到。”
“那么，”我说，“正如谚语所说，‘兄弟要伸手相助’。格劳孔如果遗漏了什么话、什么事，你就来帮他吧。不过，就我而言，他已经说出的那些，足以把我击倒，使我
english: to make some reply thereto, but his brother Adeimantus said, “You surely don’t suppose, Socrates, that the statement of the case is complete?” “Why, what else?” I said. “The very most essential point,” said he, “has not been mentioned.” “Then,” said I, “as the proverb has it, ‘Let a brother help a man’—and so, if Glaucon omits any word or deed, do you come to his aid. Though for my part what he has already said is quite enough to overthrow me and

chinese:
无力前去拯救正义了。”
“别这么说，”他说，“再听听这一点吧。要更清楚地说明我所理解的格劳孔的意思，就必须把对立一方，也就是赞扬正义、贬斥不正义的那些人的推理和言辞陈述出来。父亲们在训诫儿子时，以及所有负责照管别人的人在训诫他们照管的人时，
english:
incapacitate me for coming to the rescue of justice.” “Nonsense,” he said, “but listen to this further point. We must set forth the reasoning and the language of the opposite party, of those who commend justice and dispraise injustice, if what I conceive to be Glaucon’s meaning is to be made more clear.”

Fathers, when they address exhortations to their sons, and all those who have others in their charge,

chinese: 都劝人必须正义。他们不赞扬正义本身，赞扬的是它在人群中带来的好名声。他们给我们指明的目标，是一个人凭着显得正义，便能依靠这种名声得到官职、联姻，以及格劳孔刚才列举的、不正义者凭好名声所得的一切好处。而这些人对名声的论述还要伸展得更远。他们又加上在诸神面前的好声誉，便有说不完的福祉可供描绘；他们断言，神把这些赐给虔敬的人，正如可敬的赫西俄德和荷马所说，
english: urge the necessity of being just, not by praising justice itself, but the good repute with mankind that accrues from it, the object that they hold before us being that by seeming to be just the man may get from the reputation office and alliances and all the good things that Glaucon just now enumerated as coming to the unjust man from his good name. But those people draw out still further this topic of reputation. For, throwing in good standing with the gods, they have no lack of blessings to describe, which they affirm the gods give to pious men, even as the worthy Hesiod and Homer declare,

chinese:
前者说，神使正义者的橡树：
‘高枝结满橡实，树干中部蜂群密集。’
他又说：
‘披毛的羊群，沉甸甸地满载柔软羊毛。’
（赫西俄德《工作与时日》232 行以下）
此外，他还描述了许多类似的福祉。另一位诗人也同样说：
‘好国王敬畏高高在上的神，
统治时扶持正义与公道，黑土便献出丰饶，
english:
the one that the gods make the oaks bear for the just: ‘Acorns on topmost branches and swarms of bees on their mid-trunks,’ and he tells how the ‘Flocks of the fleece-bearing sheep are laden and weighted with soft wool,’ and of many other blessings akin to these; and similarly the other poet: ‘
Even as when a good king, who rules in the fear of the high gods,
Upholds justice and right, and the black earth yields him her foison, ’ ‘

chinese:
‘大麦、小麦蓬勃生长，树木结满美好的果实，
羊群不断繁衍，海洋也充满鱼类。’
（荷马《奥德赛》19.109）
至于神赐给正直者的福祉，穆赛俄斯和他的儿子，唱得比这些还要美妙。他们在故事中把正直者领进冥府，为圣洁的人安排宴饮；这些人头戴花冠，斜倚卧榻，
english:
Barley and wheat, and his trees are laden and weighted with fair fruits,
Increase comes to his flocks and the ocean is teeming with fishes. ’

And Musaeus and his son have a more excellent song than these of the blessings that the gods bestow on the righteous. For they conduct them to the house of Hades in their tale and arrange a symposium of the saints, where, reclined on couches crowned with wreaths,

chinese: 从此饮酒度日，仿佛德性最美好的报酬，就是永远醉酒。另一些人又把神对德性的奖赏延伸得更远。他们说，虔敬、守誓者的子子孙孙，以及后来的整个家族，将永不衰绝。他们就是用这些及类似的话赞扬正义。而对于不敬神、不正义的人，他们则把这些人埋在冥府的泥里，强迫他们用筛子汲水；趁他们还活着，
english: they entertain the time henceforth with wine, as if the fairest meed of virtue were an everlasting drunk. And others extend still further the rewards of virtue from the gods. For they say that the children’s children of the pious and oath-keeping man and his race thereafter never fail. Such and such-like are their praises of justice. But the impious and the unjust they bury in mud in the house of Hades and compel them to fetch water in a sieve, and, while they still live,

chinese:
便让他们背负恶名。格劳孔先前列举的、被误认为不正义的正义者所遭受的一切苦难，他们都拿来讲成不正义者的遭遇；除此之外，他们也没有什么可说的。他们对正义者和不正义者的赞扬与贬斥，就是这样。
“苏格拉底，再来考虑另一种关于正义和不正义的说法，
english:
they bring them into evil repute, and all the sufferings that Glaucon enumerated as befalling just men who are thought to be unjust, these they recite about the unjust, but they have nothing else to say. Such is the praise and the censure of the just and of the unjust.”

Consider further, Socrates, another kind of language about justice and injustice

chinese: 普通人和诗人都在这样说。他们众口一词，反复宣称：节制和正直固然美好、可敬，却令人不快而且辛苦；放纵和不正义则令人愉悦，容易取得，只在世人的看法和习俗中才是可耻的。他们说，大多数时候，不正义比正义更有利；而且，他们毫不犹豫地把富有或者拥有其他力量的坏人称作幸福的人，无论公开还是私下，都尊敬他们，却羞辱
english: employed by both laymen and poets. All with one accord reiterate that soberness and righteousness are fair and honorable, to be sure, but unpleasant and laborious, while licentiousness and injustice are pleasant and easy to win and are only in opinion and by convention disgraceful. They say that injustice pays better than justice, for the most part, and they do not scruple to felicitate bad men who are rich or have other kinds of power to do them honor in public and private, and to dishonor

chinese: 和轻视那些在某方面软弱或贫穷的人，即使他们也承认，这些人比前者更好。不过，在所有这些言论中，最奇怪的是他们谈论诸神和德性的话：神自己竟会把不幸和恶劣的生活分配给许多好人，却给与好人相反的人分配相反的命运。四处乞讨的祭司和占卜者来到富人家门前，使富人相信，他们通过祭祀和咒语，从神那里积蓄了一大笔力量，可以用令人愉快的节庆来赎清、消除
english: and disregard those who are in any way weak or poor, even while admitting that they are better men than the others. But the strangest of all these speeches are the things they say about the gods and virtue, how so it is that the gods themselves assign to many good men misfortunes and an evil life but to their opposites a contrary lot; and begging priests and soothsayers go to rich men’s doors and make them believe that they by means of sacrifices and incantations have accumulated a treasure of power from the gods that can expiate and cure with pleasurable festivals

chinese:
一个人或其祖先犯下的任何罪行。若有人想伤害敌人，他们又说，只要花费一点钱，无论敌人正义与否，都能加以伤害，因为他们精通咒语和法术，能强迫诸神为自己的目的效劳。他们还为所有这些话引用诗人作证。为了说明恶行容易找到、随处可得，他们引用：
‘一个人只要寻找，恶行便会大量呈现；
english:
any misdeed of a man or his ancestors, and that if a man wishes to harm an enemy, at slight cost he will be enabled to injure just and unjust alike, since they are masters of spells and enchantments that constrain the gods to serve their end. And for all these sayings they cite the poets as witnesses, with regard to the ease and plentifulness of vice, quoting: ‘
Evil-doing in plenty a man shall find for the seeking;’ ‘

chinese:
‘道路平坦，近在手边，容易踏入；
但在德性的道路上，诸神从第一步就布下汗水。’
（赫西俄德《工作与时日》287–289 行）
而且，那是一条漫长的上坡路。另一些人又援引荷马，证明人能够哄转诸神的心意，因为他也说过：
‘诸神本身也受祈祷打动，
人们借献祭和抚慰的誓愿，
english:
Smooth is the way and it lies near at hand and is easy to enter;
But on the pathway of virtue the gods put sweat from the first step, ’ and a certain long and uphill road. And others cite Homer as a witness to the beguiling of gods by men, since he too said:‘
The gods themselves are moved by prayers,
And men by sacrifice and soothing vows, ’ ‘

chinese:
‘借焚香和奠酒，转变他们的意愿；
每当犯罪越轨之后，便这样向他们祈祷。’
（荷马《伊利亚特》9.497）
他们还拿出一大堆穆赛俄斯和俄耳甫斯的书，声称两人分别是月神和缪斯的后裔；他们在仪式中使用这些书，使普通人，甚至整个城邦都相信：对于活人，通过献祭和愉快的嬉游，真的能够赦免罪行，洗清不正义的行为；
english:
And incense and libation turn their wills
Praying, whenever they have sinned and made transgression. ’ ”

And they produce a bushel of books of Musaeus and Orpheus, the offspring of the Moon and of the Muses, as they affirm, and these books they use in their ritual, and make not only ordinary men but states believe that there really are remissions of sins and purifications for deeds of injustice, by means of sacrifice and pleasant sport for the living,

chinese:
对于死者，也有专门的仪式。他们把这些称为入教仪式，说它们能把我们从另一个世界的灾难中解救出来；而那些疏于献祭的人，将面临可怕的遭遇。
“苏格拉底，人和神怎样看待德性与恶德，人们有着这一切说法。我们想想，这些话会怎样影响听者的灵魂？尤其是那些头脑敏捷的青年，他们仿佛能够从一种意见飞快地跳到另一种，从中推断出
english:
and that there are also special rites for the defunct, which they call functions, that deliver us from evils in that other world, while terrible things await those who have neglected to sacrifice.

What, Socrates, do we suppose is the effect of all such sayings about the esteem in which men and gods hold virtue and vice upon the souls that hear them, the souls of young men who are quick-witted and capable of flitting, as it were, from one expression of opinion to another and inferring from them

chinese:
一个人必须具有什么品格、采取什么道路，才能过上最好的生活。这种青年很可能会用品达的问题来问自己：
‘凭正义，还是凭弯曲的欺骗，
我才能攀上更高的城楼，
从此在围墙护卫的安稳中度过一生？’
（品达，残篇）
他们说，如果我正义，却不同时显得正义，那么，随之而来的便不是收益，而是负担、辛苦和彻底的损失；但如果我不正义，却为自己取得了正义的名声，等待我的就是神一般的生活。
english: all the character and the path whereby a man would lead the best life? Such a youth would most likely put to himself the question Pindar asks, ‘Is it by justice or by crooked deceit that I the higher tower shall scale and so live my life out in fenced and guarded security?’ The consequences of my being just are, unless I likewise seem so, not assets, they say, but liabilities, labor and total loss; but if I am unjust and have procured myself a reputation for justice a godlike life is promised.

chinese:
既然智者向我指出，是‘表象’‘压倒实在’，并且主宰幸福，那么，我就必须毫无保留地用心经营表象。（西蒙尼德斯，残篇 76，贝格克编；欧里庇得斯《俄瑞斯忒斯》236 行）为了门面和外观，我必须在自己四周勾画出一圈德性的影子，但在身后拖着极其智慧的阿尔基洛科斯所说的狐狸：狡猾多变，一心逐利。
有人会反对：做坏事的人，要永远隐藏不被发现，可不容易。我们就回答：别的任何大事，也都不容易。
english: Then since it is ‘the seeming’ as the wise men show me, that ‘masters the reality’ and is lord of happiness, to this I must devote myself without reserve. For a front and a show I must draw about myself a shadow-line of virtue, but trail behind me the fox of most sage Archilochus, shifty and bent on gain. Nay, ’tis objected, it is not easy for a wrong-doer always to lie hid. Neither is any other big thing facile,

chinese:
尽管如此，我们若想幸福，就必须循着论证的足迹所指的道路前进。为了隐藏自己，我们将组织社团和政治结社；还有善于哄人的教师，会传授在公民大会和法庭上施展的技艺。这样，我们一部分靠说服，一部分靠武力，就能设法占到便宜而不受惩罚。
可是，有人也许会说，对付诸神，无论隐瞒还是武力都无济于事。那么，如果没有诸神，或者诸神不关心人类的作为，
english: we shall reply. But all the same if we expect to be happy, we must pursue the path to which the footprints of our arguments point. For with a view to lying hid we will organize societies and political clubs, and there are teachers of cajolery who impart the arts of the popular assembly and the court-room. So that, partly by persuasion, partly by force, we shall contrive to overreach with impunity. But against the gods, it may be said, neither secrecy nor force can avail. Well, if there are no gods, or they do not concern themselves with the doings of men,

chinese: 我们也就不必费心躲开他们的察看。若诸神确实存在，而且关心这些事，我们对他们的所知和听闻，也只是来自这些言论，以及那些描述诸神谱系的诗人。但恰恰是这些权威，又告诉我们，诸神可以被说服，因“祭品和抚慰的誓愿”以及供物而改变原来的方向。我们要么两种说法都信，要么两种都不信。若要相信，那我们就该实行不正义，并从不义之财中拿出一部分献祭。
english:
neither need we concern ourselves with eluding their observation. If they do exist and pay heed, we know and hear of them only from such discourses and from the poets who have described their pedigrees. But these same authorities tell us that the gods are capable of being persuaded and swerved from their course by ‘sacrifice and soothing vows’ and dedications. We must believe them in both or neither.”

And if we are to believe them, the thing to do is to commit injustice and offer sacrifice

chinese:
因为，若我们正义，固然不会受到诸神伤害，却也把不正义的利益从自己身边推开了；若我们不正义，就能得到这些利益，而在越轨犯罪时，还能用不断的祈祷说服诸神，全身而退。
有人又会反对：但我们在这里犯下的不正义，会使我们或我们的子孙在地下世界受到审判。
我们那位精于盘算的朋友会说：“不，亲爱的先生，在这件事上，为死者举行的仪式，以及赦罪的神灵，也有很大的效力，
english: from fruits of our wrongdoing. For if we are just, we shall, it is true, be unscathed by the gods, but we shall be putting away from us the profits of injustice; but if we are unjust, we shall win those profits, and, by the importunity of our prayers, when we transgress and sin, we shall persuade them and escape scot-free. Yes, it will be objected, but we shall be brought to judgement in the world below for our unjust deeds here, we or our children’s children. ‘Nay, my dear sir,’ our calculating friend will say, ‘here again the rites for the dead have much efficacy, and the absolving divinities,

chinese:
最大的城邦都这样宣布。那些成为诗人和神谕宣告者的神之子，也向我们揭示：事实就是如此。”
“那么，我们还能根据什么理由，选择正义而不选择极端的不正义呢？只要把后者与假装的端正结合起来，按照大多数人以及最有权威者的话，我们无论生前死后，在神和人那里，都能称心如意地兴旺发达。因此，苏格拉底，听过以上这一切，一个人只要
english:
as the greatest cities declare, and the sons of gods, who became the poets and prophets of the gods, and who reveal that this is the truth.’

On what further ground, then, could we prefer justice to supreme injustice? If we combine this with a counterfeit decorum, we shall prosper to our heart’s desire, with gods and men in life and death, as the words of the multitude and of men of the highest authority declare. In consequence, then, of all that has been said, what possibility is there, Socrates, that any man

chinese: 在才智、金钱、身体或家世方面拥有可用的力量，又怎么可能同意尊重正义，而不在听到正义受赞扬时发笑呢？确实，如果有人能够揭示这些论证的错误，并且已经足够确切地知道正义最好，他会非常宽容地看待不正义者，不对他们发怒。因为他明白，除非一个人由于天性中内在的神圣而鄙弃不正义，或者由于获得知识而不去实行不正义，
english: who has the power of any resources of mind, money, body, or family should consent to honor justice and not rather laugh when he hears her praised? In sooth, if anyone is able to show the falsity of these arguments, and has come to know with sufficient assurance that justice is best, he feels much indulgence for the unjust, and is not angry with them, but is aware that except a man by inborn divinity of his nature disdains injustice, or, having won to knowledge, refrains from it,

chinese: 否则，没有别的人会自愿正义。人们只是因为缺乏勇气、年老，或者其他软弱，无力实行不正义，才贬斥它。这件事显而易见：这样的人一旦获得力量，立刻就会尽自己的能力实行不正义。而这一切的唯一原因，正是我和这位朋友向你提出整个请求时的出发点。苏格拉底，我们想指出的是：你们所有
english: no one else is willingly just, but that it is from lack of manly spirit or from old age or some other weakness that men dispraise injustice, lacking the power to practise it. The fact is patent. For no sooner does such one come into the power than he works injustice to the extent of his ability. And the sole cause of all this is the fact that was the starting-point of this entire plea of my friend here and of myself to you, Socrates, pointing out how strange it is that of all you

chinese: 自称正义辩护者的人，从言论流传至今的古代英雄，直到当今的人，没有一个在贬斥不正义或赞扬正义时，谈过别的，谈的都只是两者带来的名声、荣誉和礼物。但是，当它们处在拥有者的灵魂之中，躲过神和人的眼睛时，各自单凭其内在力量究竟是什么，却从未有人在诗歌或散文中充分说明：没有人证明，不正义是灵魂自身所含的一切恶中最大的恶，而正义则是最大的善。
english: self-styled advocates of justice, from the heroes of old whose discourses survive to the men of the present day, not one has ever censured injustice or commended justice otherwise than in respect of the repute, the honors, and the gifts that accrue from each. But what each one of them is in itself, by its own inherent force, when it is within the soul of the possessor and escapes the eyes of both gods and men, no one has ever adequately set forth in poetry or prose—the proof that the one is the greatest of all evils that the soul contains within itself, while justice is the greatest good.”

chinese: 因为，假如你们从一开始就这样说，从我们年幼时起就努力说服我们，那么，现在我们就不会只是彼此提防对方的不正义，而是每个人都成为自己最好的守卫，唯恐实行不正义，就使自己与最大的恶相伴而居。苏格拉底，色拉叙马霍斯，也许还有别人，在为正义与不正义作正反辩护时，可能会说出这些，甚至更多的话；在我看来，他们是严重颠倒了两者真正的力量。不过，我——
english: For if you had all spoken in this way from the beginning and from our youth up had sought to convince us, we should not now be guarding against one another’s injustice, but each would be his own best guardian, for fear lest by working injustice he should dwell in communion with the greatest of evils. This, Socrates, and perhaps even more than this, Thrasymachus and haply another might say in pleas for and against justice and injustice, inverting their true potencies, as I believe, grossly. But I—

chinese: 因为对你没有什么需要隐瞒——之所以竭尽全力陈述这一理论，正是因为想听你把它驳倒。不要只是用论证向我们表明正义优于不正义，还要使我们明白：两者各自单凭自身，究竟对拥有它的人做了什么，以致一个是恶，一个是善。不过，正如格劳孔所要求的，请把两者的名声都除去。因为，除非你从两者那里都拿走真实的名声，给各自安上虚假的名声，我们就会说，你赞扬的不是正义，而是它的表象，
english: for I have no reason to hide anything from you—am laying myself out to the utmost on the theory, because I wish to hear its refutation from you. Do not merely show us by argument that justice is superior to injustice, but make clear to us what each in and of itself does to its possessor, whereby the one is evil and the other good. But do away with the repute of both, as Glaucon urged. For, unless you take away from either the true repute and attach to each the false, we shall say that it is not justice that you are praising but the semblance,

chinese: 你贬斥的也不是不正义，而是它的表象；你实际上是在劝我们做不正义的事，只是要隐瞒起来。你也就和色拉叙马霍斯站在一起，认为正义是别人的好处、他人的利益，而不正义对自己有利、有益，只对弱者不利。既然你已经承认，正义属于最高的那一类善，人们既应为了其结果，也更应为了它本身而追求它，像视力、听力、理解力，是的，还有健康，
english: nor injustice that you censure, but the seeming, and that you really are exhorting us to be unjust but conceal it, and that you are at one with Thrasymachus in the opinion that justice is other man’s good, the advantage of the other, and that injustice is advantageous and profitible to oneself but disadvantageous to the inferior. Since, then, you have admitted that justice belongs to the class of those highest goods which are desirable both for their consequences and still more for their own sake, as sight, hearing, intelligence, yes and health too,

chinese: 以及一切凭自己的本性而非世人意见产生作用的好东西，那么，我希望你赞扬正义的，就是这一点：正义内在地为拥有者造成的益处，以及不正义内在地为拥有者造成的损害。至于依赖世人意见的报酬和荣誉，留给别人去赞扬吧。别人在赞扬正义、贬斥不正义时，把赞美和责备都放在两者的名声和报酬上，我尚且可以听下去；但你若这样说，除非你坚持要我接受，否则我无法接受，因为你已经用
english: and all other goods that are productive by their very nature and not by opinion, this is what I would have you praise about justice—the benefit which it and the harm which injustice inherently works upon its possessor. But the rewards and the honors that depend on opinion, leave to others to praise. For while I would listen to others who thus commended justice and disparaged injustice, bestowing their praise and their blame on the reputation and the rewards of either, I could not accept that sort of thing from you unless you say I must, because you have passed

chinese:
整个一生来思考这件事。所以我再说一次：不要仅仅从论证上向我们证明正义优于不正义，而要向我们表明，无论有没有躲过神和人的眼睛，两者各自凭自身对拥有者究竟做了什么，以致一个是善，一个是恶。”
我一向赞赏格劳孔和阿德曼托斯的天资，而这一次，
english:
your entire life in the consideration of this very matter. Do not then, I repeat, merely prove to us in argument the superiority of justice to injustice, but show us what it is that each inherently does to its possessor—whether he does or does not escape the eyes of gods and men—whereby the one is good and the other evil.”

While I had always admired the natural parts of Glaucon and Adeimantus, I was especially

chinese: 他们的话尤其让我高兴。我说：“你们这两位我们所熟识之人的儿子，有人称赞你们，真是说得极好。你们在墨伽拉战役中表现出色时，格劳孔的一位爱慕者写了一首挽歌体的诗，开篇说：‘阿里斯同的儿子，出自光荣父亲的神一般的后裔。’朋友们，我认为，这话说得好。你们能够如此为不正义辩护，却仍不相信它比正义更可取，那么，你们的性情中确实必定有几分神圣。
english:
pleased by their words on this occasion, and said: “‘
It was excellently spoken of you, sons of the man we know, ’ in the beginning of the elegy which the admirer of Glaucon wrote when you distinguished yourselves in the battle of Megara —‘Sons of Ariston, whose race from a glorious sire is god-like.’ This, my friends, I think, was well said. For there must indeed be a touch of the god-like in your disposition if you are not convinced that injustice is preferable to justice though you can plead its case in such fashion.

chinese: 而且，我相信，你们确实没有被说服。我是根据你们一贯的品格推断的；只凭你们刚才的话，我本来会怀疑你们。但我越信任你们，对这件事就越不知如何是好。我不知道该怎样前来援救正义。因为，我本以为用来反驳色拉叙马霍斯的那些论证，已经证明正义优于不正义，可你们没有接受，这使我怀疑自己的能力。另一方面，我又不知道怎么能够拒绝援救。因为我害怕，
english: And I believe that you are really not convinced. I infer this from your general character since from your words alone I should have distrusted you. But the more I trust you the more I am at a loss what to make of the matter. I do not know how I can come to the rescue. For I doubt my ability by reason that you have not accepted the arguments whereby I thought I proved against Thrasymachus that justice is better than injustice. Nor yet again do I know how I can refuse to come to the rescue. For I fear lest

chinese:
只要一个人尚有气息，还能发声，正义遭到诋毁时，却袖手旁观，胆怯退缩，不去为她辩护，这实际上就是不虔敬。因此，最好的办法，还是尽我所能帮助她。”
于是，格劳孔和其余的人都恳求我，无论如何也要来援救，不要放弃论证，而要把探究进行到底，查明两者各自的本性，以及它们各自的益处究竟如何。我便把自己的想法说出来：“我们正在着手的探究，并不容易，
english: it be actually impious to stand idly by when justice is reviled and be faint-hearted and not defend her so long as one has breath and can utter his voice. The best thing, then, is to aid her as best I can.” Glaucon, then, and the rest besought me by all means to come to the rescue and not to drop the argument but to pursue to the end the investigation as to the nature of each and the truth about their respective advantages. I said then as I thought: “The inquiry we are undertaking is no easy one but

chinese:
依我看，它需要敏锐的眼光。因此，既然我们不是什么聪明人，我想，我们应采用这样一种探究方法：假如我们的视力不很敏锐，却被要求从远处辨读细小的字；后来有人发现，同样的字，在别的地方以较大的字形写在较大的表面上，那么，我想，若能先读那些大字，再查验小字，看看是不是相同，我们一定会认为这是天赐的好运。”
“确实。”阿德曼托斯说，
english: calls for keen vision, as it seems to me. So, since we are not clever persons, I think we should employ the method of search that we should use if we, with not very keen vision, were bidden to read small letters from a distance, and then someone had observed that these same letters exist elsewhere larger and on a larger surface. We should have accounted it a godsend, I fancy, to be allowed to read those letters first, and examine the smaller, if they are the same.” “Quite so,” said Adeimantus;

chinese:
“不过，你在关于正义的探究中，看到了什么与此相似的地方？”
“我来告诉你，”我说，“我们说，一个人有正义；我想，整个城邦也有正义。”
“当然。”他说。
“城邦不是比个人更大吗？”
“更大。”他说。
“那么，在较大的对象中，正义也许更多，也更容易看清。因此，如果你们愿意，
english:
“but what analogy to do you detect in the inquiry about justice?” “I will tell you,” I said: “there is a justice of one man, we say, and, I suppose, also of an entire city.” “Assuredly,” said he. “Is not the city larger than the man?” “It is larger,” he said.

“Then, perhaps, there would be more justice in the larger object and more easy to apprehend. If it please you, then,

chinese:
我们就先在城邦中寻找正义是什么，然后再到个人身上考察它，在较小者的形态中寻找与较大者相似之处。”
“我认为这个建议好。”他说。
“那么，”我说，“如果我们的论述观察一座城邦的起源，我们也会看见正义与不正义怎样在其中产生。”
“也许。”他说。
“这样做了，我们能不能期望更容易找到所寻找的东西？”
english: let us first look for its quality in states, and then only examine it also in the individual, looking for the likeness of the greater in the form of the less.” “I think that is a good suggestion,” he said. “If, then,” said I, “our argument should observe the origin of a state, we should see also the origin of justice and injustice in it.” “It may be,” said he. “And if this is done, we may expect to find more easily what we are seeking?”

chinese:
“会容易得多。”
“那么，我们要不要试一试，把它做完？我想，这不是件小事，你们考虑一下。”
“我们考虑过了，”阿德曼托斯说，“请继续，不要推辞。”
“那么，依我看，”我说，“城邦之所以产生，是因为我们每个人都不能自给自足，而是各自缺少许多东西。你认为，建立城邦还有别的起点吗？”
“没有别的。”他说。
“所以，由于这一点，
english:
“Much more.” “Shall we try it, then, and go through with it? I fancy it is no slight task. Reflect, then.” “We have reflected,” said Adeimantus; “proceed and don’t refuse.”

“The origin of the city, then,” said I, “in my opinion, is to be found in the fact that we do not severally suffice for our own needs, but each of us lacks many things. Do you think any other principle establishes the state?” “No other,” said he. “As a result of this,

chinese:
一个人为了一种需要请来一个人，又为另一种需要请来另一个人。我们需要许多东西，便把许多人聚集在一个住处，作为伙伴和帮手；我们把这样的共同居住称为城邦或国家，不是吗？”
“正是。”
“而人与人之间，倘若有所给予、又有所取得，就发生交换，因为每个人都认为，这样对自己更好。”
“当然。”
“来吧，让我们在论述中从头建造一座城邦。看来，它真正的建造者，就是我们的需要。”
“显然。”
english: then, one man calling in another for one service and another for another, we, being in need of many things, gather many into one place of abode as associates and helpers, and to this dwelling together we give the name city or state, do we not?” “By all means.” “And between one man and another there is an interchange of giving, if it so happens, and taking, because each supposes this to be better for himself.” “Certainly.” “Come, then, let us create a city from the beginning, in our theory. Its real creator, as it appears, will be our needs.” “Obviously.”

chinese:
“我们的第一种、也是最主要的需要，是取得食物，好使生命得以存在、继续生活。”
“当然。”
“第二是住房，第三是衣服以及这类东西。”
“是这样。”
“那么请告诉我，”我说，“我们的城邦怎样才能充分提供这一切？是不是首先要有一个农夫，一个建筑工，再有一个织工？我们还要不要加上一个鞋匠，以及另一个供应身体所需之物的人？”
“当然要。”
“那么，一座城邦不可缺少的最低人数，大概就是四五个人。”
english: “Now the first and chief of our needs is the provision of food for existence and life.” “Assuredly.” “The second is housing and the third is raiment and that sort of thing.” “That is so.” “Tell me, then,” said I, “how our city will suffice for the provision of all these things. Will there not be a farmer for one, and a builder, and then again a weaver? And shall we add thereto a cobbler and some other purveyor for the needs of body?” “Certainly.” “The indispensable minimum of a city, then, would consist of four or five men.”

chinese:
“看来如此。”
“再看这一点：他们每个人是否都应把自己的劳动成果拿来供全体共同使用？我是说，农夫虽然只有一个人，是否应为四个人生产食物，为此花费四倍的时间和辛劳，再把食物分给其他人？还是不用顾及别人，只花四分之一的时间，为自己一个人生产四分之一份额
english:
“Apparently.”

“What of this, then? Shall each of these contribute his work for the common use of all? I mean shall the farmer, who is one, provide food for four and spend fourfold time and toil on the production of food and share it with the others, or shall he take no thought for them and provide a fourth portion

chinese:
的食物，其余四分之三的时间，一部分用来建房，一部分用来制衣，一部分用来做鞋，不必麻烦自己同别人合作，而是自己为自己，只管自己的事？”
阿德曼托斯说：“不过，苏格拉底，也许前一种办法比较容易。”
“宙斯在上，这毫不奇怪，”我说，“你这么一提，我自己也想到了：首先，我们各人的天性并非
english: of the food for himself alone in a quarter of the time and employ the other three-quarters, the one in the provision of a house, the other of a garment, the other of shoes, and not have the bother of associating with other people, but, himself for himself, mind his own affairs?” And Adeimantus said, “But, perhaps, Socrates, the former way is easier.” “It would not, by Zeus, be at all strange,” said I; “for now that you have mentioned it, it occurs to me myself that, to begin with, our several natures are not

chinese:
完全相同，而是各有不同。一个人天生适合一种工作，另一个人适合另一种。你不这样认为吗？”
“我也这样认为。”
“再说，一个人同时做许多工作，还是一个人专做一种工作，会做得更好？”
“一个人专做一种。”他说。
“而且，我想，这一点显而易见：任何工作，若错过了合适的时节、有利的时机，工作就会弄坏。”
“显而易见。”
“我想，这是因为工作不会等待工匠有空闲，反而是工匠必须
english: all alike but different. One man is naturally fitted for one task, and another for another. Don’t you think so?” “I do.” “Again, would one man do better working at many tasks or one at one?” “One at one,” he said. “And, furthermore, this, I fancy, is obvious—that if one lets slip the right season, the favorable moment in any task, the work is spoiled.” “Obvious.” “That, I take it, is because the business will not wait upon the leisure of the workman, but the workman must

chinese:
把它当作主要事务来照料，而不能把它当成顺便做的副业。”
“确实必须这样。”
“那么，结果就是：一个人按照自己的天性，在恰当的时机专做一种工作，不被其他事务分心，生产出来的东西就会更多、更好，也更容易。”
“正是。”
“那么，阿德曼托斯，要提供我们说过的那些东西，所需的公民便不止四个人了。因为看来，农夫若要有一副好犁，就不会自己制造，
english: attend to it as his main affair, and not as a by-work.” “He must indeed.” “The result, then, is that more things are produced, and better and more easily when one man performs one task according to his nature, at the right moment, and at leisure from other occupations.” “By all means.” “Then, Adeimantus, we need more than four citizens for the provision of the things we have mentioned. For the farmer, it appears, will not make his own plough if it is to be a good one,

chinese:
锄头和其他农具也一样；建筑工也不会亲自制造自己的工具，而他需要的工具同样很多。织工和鞋匠也是如此。”
“对。”
“因此，木匠、铁匠以及许多类似的工匠，加入我们的小村落，就会使它扩大不少。”
“当然。”
“但它仍不会很大，即使我们再添上牧牛人、牧羊人和其他牧人，
english: nor his hoe, nor his other agricultural implements, nor will the builder, who also needs many; and similarly the weaver and cobbler.” “True.” “Carpenters, then, and smiths and many similar craftsmen, associating themselves with our hamlet, will enlarge it considerably.” “Certainly.” “Yet it still wouldn’t be very large even if we should add to them neat-herds and shepherds and other herders,

chinese:
让农夫有牛来耕地，让建筑工有牛同农夫一起运输东西，让织工和鞋匠有皮革和羊毛可用。”
“若全都有了，那也算不上一座小城邦了。”
“不过，”我说，“要把城邦建在一个完全不需要进口的地方，几乎是不可能的。”
“确实。”
“那么，我们还会需要一些人，从别的城邦运来所需的东西。”
“会需要。”
“再说，如果替我们办事的人空手出发，没有带上任何对方所需要的东西，
english:
so that the farmers might have cattle for ploughing, and the builders oxen to use with the farmers for transportation, and the weavers and cobblers hides and fleeces for their use.” “It wouldn’t be a small city, either, if it had all these.” “But further,” said I, “it is practically impossible to establish the city in a region where it will not need imports.” “It is.” “There will be a further need, then, of those who will bring in from some other city what it requires.” “There will.”

“And again, if our servitor goes forth empty-handed, not taking with him any of the things needed by those

chinese:
也就是没有带上那些向我们提供所需之物的人需要的东西，那么，他也会空手回来，不是吗？”
“我想会的。”
“因此，我们在本地的生产，就不能只满足自己，还必须在种类和数量上，满足那些我们需要与之往来的人的需要。”
“必须如此。”
“所以，我们的城邦需要更多农夫和其他工匠。”
“是，需要更多。”
“还需要另一些服务者，负责货物的输出和输入。他们就是商人，不是吗？”
“是。”
“那么，我们也需要商人。”
“当然。”
“如果贸易通过海路进行，
english: from whom they procure what they themselves require, he will come back with empty hands, will he not?” “I think so.” “Then their home production must not merely suffice for themselves but in quality and quantity meet the needs of those of whom they have need.” “It must.” “So our city will require more farmers and other craftsmen.” “Yes, more.” “And also of other ministrants who are to export and import the merchandise. These are traders, are they not?” “Yes.” “We shall also need traders, then.” “Assuredly.” “And if the trading is carried on by sea,

chinese:
我们还需要相当多精通航海事务的人。”
“相当多。”
“可是，在城邦内部，他们又怎样彼此分享劳动的产品？我们结成伙伴、建立城邦，本来就是为了这个目的。”
“显然，”他说，“通过买卖。”
“那么，由此就会产生市场，以及作为交换凭证的货币。”
english:
we shall need quite a number of others who are expert in maritime business.” “Quite a number.”

“But again, within the city itself how will they share with one another the products of their labor? This was the very purpose of our association and establishment of a state.” “Obviously,” he said, “by buying and selling.” “A market-place, then, and money as a token for the purpose of exchange will be the result of this.”

chinese:
“正是。”
“那么，农夫或其他工匠带着产品来到市场，如果到达的时间同想和他交换的人不一致，他是不是就该在市场上闲坐着，耽误自己的工作时间？”
“绝不是，”他说，“会有人看出这种需要，自愿承担这项服务。在管理良好的城邦里，他们通常是身体最弱、不能胜任其他工作的人。他们必须留在市场上，
english: “By all means.” “If, then, the farmer or any other craftsman taking his products to the market-place does not arrive at the same time with those who desire to exchange with him, is he to sit idle in the market-place and lose time from his own work?” “By no means,” he said, “but there are men who see this need and appoint themselves for this service—in well-conducted cities they are generally those who are weakest in body and those who are useless for any other task. They must wait there in the agora

chinese:
对想卖东西的人，用钱换取货物；对想买东西的人，用货物换取钱。”
“那么，”我说，“这种需要就在我们的城邦中产生了零售商这一类人。那些留在市场里，为我们从事买卖的人，我们不正是称他们为零售商，而把往来各城邦之间的人称为贸易商吗？”
“当然。”
“此外，我想，还有另一些服务者，他们在心智方面
english: and exchange money for goods with those who wish to sell, and goods for money with as many as desire to buy.” “This need, then,” said I, “creates the class of shopkeepers in our city. Or is not shopkeepers the name we give to those who, planted in the agora, serve us in buying and selling, while we call those who roam from city to city merchants?” “Certainly.” “And there are, furthermore, I believe, other servitors who in the things of the mind

chinese:
不完全配成为我们的伙伴，但身体的力量足以从事劳作。他们出售这种力量的使用，把所得的价钱称为工资，因此，我想，人们称他们为雇工，不是吗？”
“当然。”
“那么，看来雇工便是使城邦充实完整的补充。”
“我想是的。”
“阿德曼托斯，我们的城邦现在已经长成，已经完整了吗？”
“也许。”
“那么，在它里面，哪里可以找到正义和不正义？它们随着我们已经考察的哪些组成部分进入城邦？”
english: are not altogether worthy of our fellowship, but whose strength of body is sufficient for toil; so they, selling the use of this strength and calling the price wages, are designated, I believe, wage-earners, are they not?” “Certainly.” “Wage-earners, then, it seems, are the complement that helps to fill up the state.” “I think so.” “Has our city, then, Adeimantus, reached its full growth and is it complete?” “Perhaps.” “Where, then, can justice and injustice be found in it? And along with which of the constituents that we have considered does it come into the state?”

chinese:
“苏格拉底，我想不出来，”他说，“除非就在这些组成部分彼此需要的某种关系之中。”
“也许这个建议不错，”我说，“我们必须查验，不要退缩。那么，首先让我们考虑：这样得到供应的人，将过怎样的生活？他们不是会制作面包、酒、衣服和鞋子吗？他们还会为自己建造房屋，夏天工作时大多不穿衣、不穿鞋，冬天则穿衣，
english: “I cannot conceive, Socrates,” he said, “unless it be in some need that those very constituents have of one another.” “Perhaps that is a good suggestion,” said I; “we must examine it and not hold back. First of all, then, let us consider what will be the manner of life of men thus provided. Will they not make bread and wine and garments and shoes? And they will build themselves houses and carry on their work in summer for the most part unclad and unshod and in winter clothed and

chinese: 穿鞋，足以御寒？他们把大麦磨成粗面，把小麦磨成面粉，揉好烤熟，在铺好的芦苇或干净树叶上摆出上好的面饼和面包，斜倚在铺着泻根藤和桃金娘的乡间草榻上，同孩子们一起享用。他们喝着自己的酒，戴着花冠，在愉快的相聚中唱歌颂神；他们生养的子女不超过自己的供养能力，以免陷入贫困或战争，不是吗？”
english: shod sufficiently? And for their nourishment they will provide meal from their barley and flour from their wheat, and kneading and cooking these they will serve noble cakes and loaves on some arrangement of reeds or clean leaves, and, reclined on rustic beds strewn with bryony and myrtle, they will feast with their children, drinking of their wine thereto, garlanded and singing hymns to the gods in pleasant fellowship, not begetting offspring beyond their means lest they fall into poverty or war?”

chinese:
这时格劳孔插话说：“看来，你描述的这些赴宴的人，连佐餐的小菜也没有。”
“对，”我说，“我忘了，他们也会有小菜。当然，有盐、橄榄、奶酪、洋葱和蔬菜；乡下人煮来吃的那些东西，他们都会放在一起煮。至于餐后的食品，我们给他们无花果、鹰嘴豆和蚕豆，
english: Here Glaucon broke in: “No relishes apparently,” he said, “for the men you describe as feasting.” “True” said I; “I forgot that they will also have relishes—salt, of course, and olives and cheese and onions and greens, the sort of things they boil in the country, they will boil up together. But for dessert we will serve them figs and chickpeas and beans,

chinese:
他们还会在火前烤桃金娘果和橡实，配着适量的酒喝下去。这样，他们平安、健康地生活，大概会寿终正寝，把同样的生活传给子孙。”
他说：“苏格拉底，如果你要建立一座猪的城邦，你给它们预备的饲料，除了这些还能有什么？”
“那么，格劳孔，你想要什么？”我问。
“通常有的那些东西，”他回答，“要是不想让他们不舒服，我想，他们就必须斜倚卧榻，
english: and they will toast myrtle-berries and acorns before the fire, washing them down with moderate potations and so, living in peace and health, they will probably die in old age and hand on a like life to their offspring.” And he said, “If you were founding a city of pigs, Socrates, what other fodder than this would you provide?” “Why, what would you have, Glaucon?” said I. “What is customary,” he replied; “They must recline on couches, I presume, if they are not to be uncomfortable,

chinese:
在餐桌旁用饭，吃如今常见的精制菜肴和甜食。”
“好，”我说，“我明白了。看来，我们考察的不只是城邦的起源，而是一座奢华城邦的起源。也许这个建议也不坏。观察这样一座城邦，我们或许能辨认出，正义和不正义怎样在城邦中产生。我相信，真正的城邦是刚才描述的那一种，也就是健康的城邦。不过，如果你们愿意再考察一座发热的城邦，也没有什么妨碍。
english: and dine from tables and have made dishes and sweetmeats such as are now in use.” “Good,” said I, “I understand. It is not merely the origin of a city, it seems, that we are considering but the origin of a luxurious city. Perhaps that isn’t such a bad suggestion, either. For by observation of such a city it may be we could discern the origin of justice and injustice in states. The true state I believe to be the one we have described—the healthy state, as it were. But if it is your pleasure that we contemplate also a fevered state, there is nothing to hinder.”

chinese: 看来，有些人不会满足于那样的饭食和那样的生活；必须再加上卧榻、餐桌和其他家具，还有小菜、没药、香料、姑娘和糕点——每一种都要有各式各样。我们最初提到的需要，即房屋、衣服和鞋子，也不再限于必需；我们必须让绘画和刺绣的技艺开工，取得黄金、象牙以及类似的装饰品，不是吗？”
english: For there are some, it appears, who will not be contented with this sort of fare or with this way of life; but couches will have to be added thereto and tables and other furniture, yes, and relishes and myrrh and incense and girls and cakes—all sorts of all of them. And the requirements we first mentioned, houses and garments and shoes, will no longer be confined to necessities, but we must set painting to work and embroidery, and procure gold and ivory and similar adornments, must we not?”

chinese:
“是的。”他说。
“那么，我们就得再次扩大城邦。那个健康的城邦已经不够，我们必须继续使它膨胀，用许多超过城邦必要需求的东西把它填满。例如，整个猎人群体，还有模仿者：许多人从事形象和色彩的模仿，许多人从事诗乐的模仿——诗人及其助手、史诗吟诵者、演员、歌舞队员、演出承办者；还有
english: “Yes,” he said. “Then we shall have to enlarge the city again. For that healthy state is no longer sufficient, but we must proceed to swell out its bulk and fill it up with a multitude of things that exceed the requirements of necessity in states, as, for example, the entire class of huntsmen, and the imitators, many of them occupied with figures and colors and many with music—the poets and their assistants, rhapsodists, actors, chorus-dancers, contractors—and

chinese: 各种物品的制造者，尤其是与妇女装饰有关的物品。这样，我们也会需要更多服务者。你不认为，我们会需要儿童监护人、奶妈和保姆、美容的妇人、理发师，另外还有厨师和掌勺的大厨吗？我们还需要养猪人；在先前的城邦中，没有这一类人，因为我们不需要他们，而在这座城邦里，这种需要也会出现。若要吃肉，我们也会需要大量其他牲畜，不是吗？”
english: the manufacturers of all kinds of articles, especially those that have to do with women’s adornment. And so we shall also want more servitors. Don’t you think that we shall need tutors, nurses wet and dry, beauty-shop ladies, barbers and yet again cooks and chefs? And we shall have need, further, of swineherds; there were none of these creatures in our former city, for we had no need of them, but in this city there will be this further need; and we shall also require other cattle in great numbers if they are to be eaten, shall we not?”

chinese:
“是的。”
“如果这样生活，和先前相比，我们是不是也会更需要医生的服务？”
“多得多。”
“我想，先前足以养活当时人口的土地，就会由充足变得太小了。是不是这样？”
“是。”
“那么，为了有足够的牧场和耕地，我们就得割取邻国的一块土地；如果邻国也任凭自己无限追求财富，
english:
“Yes.” “Doctors, too, are something whose services we shall be much more likely to require if we live thus than as before?” “Much.”

“And the territory, I presume, that was then sufficient to feed the then population, from being adequate will become too small. Is that so or not?” “It is.” “Then we shall have to cut out a cantle of our neighbor’s land if we are to have enough for pasture and ploughing, and they in turn of ours if they too abandon themselves to the unlimited acquisition of wealth,

chinese:
不顾必要需求所划定的限度，它们也会反过来割取我们的土地。”
“苏格拉底，这是不可避免的。”
“格劳孔，下一步我们就会打仗，还是会发生别的什么事？”
“就会发生你说的事。”他说。
“不过，”我说，“我们现在还不谈战争有什么坏处或好处，只确认我们又发现了战争的起源：它来自那些在出现时，会给城邦带来最大公共灾难和私人灾难的事物。”
“当然。”
“那么，朋友，我们还得进一步扩大城邦，
english:
disregarding the limit set by our necessary wants.” “Inevitably, Socrates.” “We shall go to war as the next step, Glaucon—or what will happen?” “What you say,” he said. “And we are not yet to speak,” said I, “of any evil or good effect of war, but only to affirm that we have further discovered the origin of war, namely, from those things from which the greatest disasters, public and private, come to states when they come.” “Certainly.”

“Then, my friend, we must still further enlarge our city

chinese:
而且不是稍稍增加，而是要增加一整支军队。他们将出城，同进攻者战斗，保卫我们全部的财富和刚才描述的奢华生活。”
“为什么？”他说，“公民自己还不足以做这件事吗？”
“如果你和我们大家，”我说，“在塑造城邦时所承认的原则是对的，那就不够。你记得吧，我们确实同意，一个人不可能把许多种技艺的工作都做好。”
“对。”他说。
“那么，”我说，
english: by no small increment, but by a whole army, that will march forth and fight it out with assailants in defence of all our wealth and the luxuries we have just described.” “How so?” he said; “are the citizens themselves not sufficient for it?” “Not if you,” said I, “and we all were right in the admission we made when we were molding our city. We surely agreed, if you remember, that it is impossible for one man to do the work of many arts well.” “True,” he said. “Well, then,” said I,

chinese:
“你不认为，打仗的事务也是一种技艺和专门职业吗？”
“确实是。”他说。
“那么，我们对制鞋技艺的关心，应当大于对战争技艺的关心吗？”
“绝不应当。”
“我们为了把鞋做好，费心不让鞋匠同时尝试当农夫、织工或建筑工，要他专做鞋匠；同样，我们给每一个人都分派一项他适合、天性相宜的工作，让他一生都从事这项工作，
english: “don’t you think that the business of fighting is an art and a profession?” “It is indeed,” he said. “Should our concern be greater, then, for the cobbler’s art than for the art of war?” “By no means.” “Can we suppose, then, that while we were at pains to prevent the cobbler from attempting to be at the same time a farmer, a weaver, or a builder instead of just a cobbler, to the end that we might have the cobbler’s business well done, and similarly assigned to each and every one man one occupation, for which he was fit and naturally adapted and at which he was to work all his days,

chinese: 不被其他事务分心，也不错过把工作做好的恰当时机。难道我们这样做了，却还要怀疑，把战争事务做好是不是最重要的事？难道打仗如此容易，一个耕地的人可以同时成为士兵，做鞋或从事其他行业的人也一样？可是，任何人若不是从小就专门练习棋戏或骰戏，而只把它当作偶尔做的事，根本不可能成为胜任的高手。难道我们还应当相信，一个人只要
english: at leisure from other pursuits and not letting slip the right moments for doing the work well, and that yet we are in doubt whether the right accomplishment of the business of war is not of supreme moment? Is it so easy that a man who is cultivating the soil will be at the same time a soldier and one who is practising cobbling or any other trade, though no man in the world could make himself a competent expert at draughts or the dice who did not practise that and nothing else from childhood but treated it as an occasional business? And are we to believe that a man who

chinese:
拿起盾牌或其他战争器具，就在当天成了合格的重装战士，或擅长其他战斗方式的人？但没有任何别的工具，会因为一个人把它拿到手里，就使他成为工匠或竞技选手；对既未掌握有关知识、又没有充分练习其用法的人，工具也不会有什么帮助。”
“如果真能那样，”他说，“工具的价值可太大了。”
“那么，”我说，“我们的护卫者承担的任务，既然比一切任务都更重大，
english:
takes in hand a shield or any other instrument of war springs up on that very day a competent combatant in heavy armor or in any other form of warfare—though no other tool will make a man be an artist or an athlete by his taking it in hand, nor will it be of any service to those who have neither acquired the science of it nor sufficiently practised themselves in its use?” “Great indeed,” he said, “would be the value of tools in that case.”

“Then,” said I, “in the same degree that the task of our guardians is the greatest of all,

chinese:
就应比任何其他事务都更需要不受杂务分心，也更需要最高的知识和训练。”
“我想是的。”他说。
“它不也需要适合这项工作的天性吗？”
“当然。”
“那么，看来我们的任务，就是尽我们所能，挑选出哪些天性、哪一类天性适合守卫城邦。”
“是，我们的任务。”
“说真的，”我说，“我们给自己承担的，不是件轻松的工作。不过，只要力量还允许，我们就不能泄气。”
english: it would require more leisure than any other business and the greatest science and training.” “I think so,” said he. “Does it not also require a nature adapted to that very pursuit?” “Of course.” “It becomes our task, then, it seems, if we are able, to select which and what kind of natures are suited for the guardianship of a state.” “Yes, ours.” “Upon my word,” said I, “it is no light task that we have taken upon ourselves. But we must not faint so far as our strength allows.”

chinese:
“是，不能。”
“你认为，”我说，“就守卫的工作而言，一条良种猎犬的天性，同一个禀赋优良的青年，有什么区别吗？”
“你指的是哪一点？”
“我是说，两者都必须感知敏锐，发现目标后追赶迅速，而且如果必须同捕获的对象搏斗，还得强壮有力。”
“是的，”他说，“这些品质都需要。”
“并且，要善于战斗，还必须勇敢。”
“当然。”
“可是，一种生物若没有旺盛的激情，能够勇敢吗？无论是马、狗，还是
english: “No, we mustn’t.” “Do you think,” said I, “that there is any difference between the nature of a well-bred hound for this watch-dog’s work and of a well-born lad?” “What point have you in mind?” “I mean that each of them must be keen of perception, quick in pursuit of what it has apprehended, and strong too if it has to fight it out with its captive.” “Why, yes,” said he, “there is need of all these qualities.” “And it must, further, be brave if it is to fight well.” “Of course.” “And will a creature be ready to be brave that is not high-spirited, whether horse or dog or

chinese:
其他任何生物？你难道从未注意过，激情是一种多么不可抗拒、不可战胜的力量？只要有它，每个灵魂面对一切都无所畏惧，不能被征服。”
“我注意过。”
“那么，护卫者应具备的身体品质，已经清楚了。”
“是的。”
“灵魂的品质也清楚了：他必须激情旺盛。”
“是，这也清楚了。”
“那么，格劳孔，”我说，“如果他们具有这样的天性，又怎样才能避免凶狠地对待彼此和其他公民呢？”
“宙斯在上，不容易。”他说。
“然而，
english: anything else? Have you never observed what an irresistible and invincible thing is spirit, the presence of which makes every soul in the face of everything fearless and unconquerable?” “I have.” “The physical qualities of the guardian, then, are obvious.” “Yes.” “And also those of his soul, namely that he must be of high spirit.” “Yes, this too.” “How then, Glaucon,” said I, “will they escape being savage to one another and to the other citizens if this is to be their nature?” “Not easily, by Zeus,” said he. “And yet

chinese:
我们必须让他们对朋友温和，对敌人严厉；否则，他们不用等别人来毁灭城邦，自己就会先把它毁灭。”
“对。”他说。
“那么，我们该怎么办？”我说，“在哪里能找到一种既温和、又激情旺盛的性情呢？因为激情旺盛与天性温和，看起来是相反的。”
“是这样。”
“然而，缺少这两种品质中的任何一种，他都永远不能成为好的护卫者。但这些要求似乎不可能同时实现，所以，
english: we must have them gentle to their friends and harsh to their enemies; otherwise they will not await their destruction at the hands of others, but will be first themselves in bringing it about.” “True,” he said. “What, then, are we to do?” said I. “Where shall we discover a disposition that is at once gentle and great-spirited? For there appears to be an opposition between the spirited type and the gentle nature.” “There does.” “But yet if one lacks either of these qualities, a good guardian he never can be. But these requirements resemble impossibilities, and so

chinese:
结果便是，好的护卫者不可能存在。”
“看来是这样。”他说。
我陷入了困境，重新思量我们刚才的话之后，我说：“朋友，我们陷入困惑，也是活该，因为我们忘记了自己提出的那个比照。”
“你是什么意思？”
“我们没有注意到：那种我们以为不可能的天性，毕竟是存在的，它同时具有这些相反的品质。”
“在哪里？”
“在其他动物身上可以看到，尤其是我们曾拿来
english: the result is that a good guardian is impossible.” “It seems likely,” he said. And I was at a standstill, and after reconsidering what we had been saying, I said, “We deserve to be at a loss, my friend, for we have lost sight of the comparison that we set before ourselves.” “What do you mean?” “We failed to note that there are after all such natures as we thought impossible, endowed with these opposite qualities.” “Where?” “It may be observed in other animals, but especially in that which we

chinese:
比作护卫者的那一种动物。你一定注意过，良种猎犬的自然性情，对熟悉的人、认识的人极其温和，对不认识的人却恰恰相反。”
“我知道。”
