“那么看这一点：如果某种东西离开了自己的形态，它不就是被自身或别的东西移离原状、加以改变了吗？”
english: “And what of this, the second. Do you think that God is a wizard and capable of manifesting himself by design, now in one aspect, now in another, at one time himself changing and altering his shape in many transformations and at another deceiving us and causing us to believe such things about him; or that he is simple and less likely than anything else to depart from his own form?” “I cannot say offhand,” he replied. “But what of this: If anything went out from its own form, would it not be displaced and changed, either by itself or by something else?”

chinese:
“必然如此。”
“处于最佳状态的东西，不是最不容易被外物改变和动摇吗？例如，身体受到饮食和劳累影响，植物受到日晒、风吹以及类似因素影响，不是越健康、越强壮，就越不容易改变吗？”
english:
“Necessarily.” “Is it not true that to be altered and moved by something else happens least to things that are in the best condition, ”

as, for example, a body by food and drink and toil, and plants by the heat of the sun and winds and similar influences—is it not true that the healthiest and strongest is least altered?”

chinese:
“当然。”
“灵魂也是如此：最勇敢、最有理解力的灵魂，不是最不容易被外来的影响扰动和改变吗？”
“是的。”
“同样的道理，对于一切组合而成的器具、建筑和衣物，也确实成立：制造精良、状态良好的，最不容易被时间和其他因素改变。”
“是这样。”
“因此，普遍说来，一种东西，若凭天性，或凭
english: “Certainly.” “And is it not the soul that is bravest and most intelligent, that would be least disturbed and altered by any external affection?” “Yes.” “And, again, it is surely true of all composite implements, edifices, and habiliments, by parity of reasoning, that those which are well made and in good condition are least liable to be changed by time and other influences.” “That is so.” “It is universally true, then, that that which is in the best state by nature or

chinese:
技艺，或凭两者而处于最佳状态，就最不容易被别的东西改变。”
“看来如此。”
“可是，神以及一切属于神的东西，在每一方面都必定处于可能的最佳状态。”
“当然。”
“那么，从这一方面看，神就最不可能具有多种形态。”
“确实最不可能。”
“但他会不会改变自身，使自己变形？”
“如果他发生变化，”他说，“显然就只能如此。”
“那么，他改变自己，是变得更好，比原来更美，还是变得更坏，比原来更丑呢？”
english:
art or both admits least alteration by something else.” “So it seems.” “But God, surely, and everything that belongs to God is in every way in the best possible state.” “Of course.” “From this point of view, then, it would be least of all likely that there would be many forms in God.” “Least indeed.”

“But would he transform and alter himself?” “Obviously,” he said, “if he is altered.” “Then does he change himself for the better and to something fairer, or for the worse and to something uglier than himself?”

chinese:
“如果他改变，”他说，“必定是变得更坏。因为我们当然不能说，神在美或完善方面还有欠缺。”
“说得极对，”我说，“阿德曼托斯，如果情况如此，你认为，无论神还是人，会有谁自愿使自己在任何方面变得更坏吗？”
“不可能。”他回答。
“那么，”我说，“即使是神，也不可能希望改变自己；看来，每一位神都已经尽可能地美好和完善，因此永远单纯地保持自己的形态。”
“依我看，这是绝对必然的结论。”
“那么，任何诗人，”
english: “It must necessarily,” said he, “be for the worse if he is changed. For we surely will not say that God is deficient in either beauty or excellence.” “Most rightly spoken,” said I. “And if that were his condition, do you think, Adeimantus, that any one god or man would of his own will worsen himself in any way?” “Impossible,” he replied. “It is impossible then,” said I, “even for a god to wish to alter himself, but, as it appears, each of them being the fairest and best possible abides for ever simply in his own form.” “An absolutely necessary conclusion to my thinking.” “No poet then,”

chinese:
我说，“好朋友，我们都不能容许他告诉我们：
‘诸神装成陌生人的模样，
变换种种伪装，走访凡人的城邦。’
（荷马《奥德赛》17.485–486）
也不能让任何人编造关于普罗透斯和忒提斯的谎言，或在悲剧及其他诗作中，让赫拉乔装成女祭司，为‘阿尔戈斯的河流伊那科斯那些赐予生命的儿子’募集捐献。（埃斯库罗斯）
english:
I said, “my good friend, must be allowed to tell us that ‘
The gods, in the likeness of strangers,
Many disguises assume as they visit the cities of mortals.’ Nor must anyone tell falsehoods about Proteus and Thetis, nor in any tragedy or in other poems bring in Hera disguised as a priestess collecting alms ‘
for the life-giving sons of Inachus, the Argive stream. ’

chinese:
其他许多类似的谎言，他们也不能讲。母亲们也不能受这些诗人影响，用有害的故事恐吓孩子，说有些神会在夜间出没，化作来自各地的种种陌生人；否则，她们在诋毁诸神的同时，也把孩子变得胆怯。”
“不能这样。”他说。
“不过，”我说，“我们能不能设想：诸神本身虽然不能改变，却用欺骗和法术对付我们，使我们以为他们以许多形态出现？”
“也许。”他说。
english: And many similar falsehoods they must not tell. Nor again must mothers under the influence of such poets terrify their children with harmful tales, how that there are certain gods whose apparitions haunt the night in the likeness of many strangers from all manner of lands, lest while they speak evil of the gods they at the same time make cowards of children.” “They must not,” he said. “But,” said I, “may we suppose that while the gods themselves are incapable of change they cause us to fancy that they appear in many shapes deceiving and practising magic upon us?” “Perhaps,” said he.

chinese:
“考虑一下，”我说，“神会愿意在言语或行动中展示仅仅是表象的东西，以此欺骗或说谎吗？”
“我不知道。”他说。
“你不知道，”我说，“如果可以这样表达，那种真正的虚假，是所有神和人都憎恶的东西吗？”
“你是什么意思？”他问。
“我是说，”我说，“没有人愿意在自身最重要的部分，对自己最重要的事情，接受虚假；恰恰是在那里，人人最害怕虚假。”
“我还是不懂。”
“那是因为你以为我在说什么高深的意思，”
english: “Consider,” said I; “would a god wish to deceive, or lie, by presenting in either word or action what is only appearance?” “I don’t know,” said he. “Don’t you know,” said I, “that the veritable lie, if the expression is permissible, is a thing that all gods and men abhor?” “What do you mean?” he said. “This,” said I, “that falsehood in the most vital part of themselves, and about their most vital concerns, is something that no one willingly accepts, but it is there above all that everyone fears it.” “I don’t understand yet either.” “That is because you suspect me of some grand meaning,”

chinese:
我说，“其实我说的是：灵魂对真实事物受到欺骗，受蒙蔽而盲目无知，把虚假留在其中，始终持有它，这是人人最不愿接受的；也正是在这种情况下，人最憎恶虚假。”
“确实。”他说。
“不过，正如我刚才所说，把这称为真正的虚假，也就是受骗者灵魂中的无知，才是完全恰当的。因为言辞中的虚假，是灵魂所受状态的摹本，
english: I said; “but what I mean is, that deception in the soul about realities, to have been deceived and to be blindly ignorant and to have and hold the falsehood there, is what all men would least of all accept, and it is in that case that they loathe it most of all.” “Quite so,” he said. “But surely it would be most wholly right, as I was just now saying, to describe this as in very truth falsehood—ignorance namely in the soul of the man deceived. For the falsehood in words is a copy of the affection in the soul,

chinese:
是随后产生的影像，并非完全纯粹的虚假。不是这样吗？”
“正是。”
“那么，这种本质上的虚假，不仅为神，也为人所憎恶。”
“我同意。”
“可是，言辞中的虚假又怎样呢？它在什么时候、对什么人会有用，以致不该受到憎恶？对付敌人时，不会有用吗？还有，当那些我们称为朋友的人，由于疯狂或愚蠢，企图做出什么恶事时，它不就会成为有用的东西，
english:
an after-rising image of it and not an altogether unmixed falsehood. Is not that so?” “By all means.”

“Essential falsehood, then, is hated not only by gods but by men.” “I agree.” “But what of the falsehood in words, when and for whom is it serviceable so as not to merit abhorrence? Will it not be against enemies? And when any of those whom we call friends owing to madness or folly attempts to do some wrong, does it not then become useful

chinese:
像药物一样，阻止恶事发生吗？再说，刚才谈到的寓言，由于我们不了解古代的真相，便尽可能使虚构近似真实，从而让它有益于教导。”
“我们确实如此。”他说。
“那么请告诉我：在这些理由中，有哪一种能使虚假对神有用？难道神会因为不了解古代，而编造它的虚假影像吗？”
“这个设想太荒谬了。”他说。
“那么，神里面没有说谎的诗人。”
“我想没有。”
english: to avert the evil—as a medicine? And also in the fables of which we were just now speaking owing to our ignorance of the truth about antiquity, we liken the false to the true as far as we may and so make it edifying.” “We most certainly do,” he said. “Tell me, then, on which of these grounds falsehood would be serviceable to God. Would he because of his ignorance of antiquity make false likenesses of it?” “An absurd supposition, that,” he said. “Then there is no lying poet in God.” “I think not.”

chinese:
“那么，他会因为害怕敌人而说谎吗？”
“远不会。”
“会因为朋友的愚蠢或疯狂吗？”
“不会，没有愚人或疯子是神的朋友。”
“那么，神没有欺骗的动机。”
“没有。”
“从任何方面看，神圣之物和神本身，都没有虚假。”
“正是。”
“那么，神在行动和言语上都完全单纯、真实；他既不改变自身，也不用幻象、言辞，或在人醒着及梦中发出的征兆欺骗别人。”
english:
“Well then, would it be through fear of his enemies that he would lie?” “Far from it.” “Would it be because of the folly or madness of his friends?” “Nay, no fool or madman is a friend of God.” “Then there is no motive for God to deceive.” “None.” “From every point of view the divine and the divinity are free from falsehood.” “By all means.”

“Then God is altogether simple and true in deed and word, and neither changes himself nor deceives others by visions or words or the sending of signs in waking or in dreams.”

chinese:
“听你这样说，”他说，“我自己也这样认为。”
“那么，”我说，“你赞同把这一点定为谈论诸神的言辞和诗歌的第二条规范或准则：诸神既不是会变换形体的魔术师，也不用言行中的虚假误导我们？”
“我赞同。”
“那么，荷马虽有许多别的地方值得我们赞扬，但宙斯给阿伽门农送去那个梦的故事，我们不会赞许；埃斯库罗斯让忒提斯说出下面这番话，我们也不会赞同：
english: “I myself think so,” he said, “when I hear you say it.” “You concur then,” I said, “this as our second norm or canon for speech and poetry about the gods,—that they are neither wizards in shape-shifting nor do they mislead us by falsehoods in words or deed?” “I concur.” “Then, though there are many other things that we praise in Homer, this we will not applaud, the sending of the dream by Zeus to Agamemnon, nor shall we approve of Aeschylus when his Thetis avers that

chinese:
阿波罗在她的婚礼上歌唱，曾‘预言她的孩子命运幸福’：
‘寿命绵长，没有痛苦与疾病，
他把上天的一切福祉讲述完毕，
又高唱庄严的颂歌，使我心中欢喜。
我相信，福玻斯那充满神谕气息的
神圣之口，不可能说谎。
可是，他本人，那歌唱者；他本人，
曾与我们同席用餐的人；他本人，许诺了一切的人，
如今却亲自杀死了我的儿子。’
（埃斯库罗斯，残篇 350）
english:
Apollo singing at her wedding, ‘foretold the happy fortunes of her issue’ — ‘
Their days prolonged, from pain and sickness free,
And rounding out the tale of heaven’s blessings,
Raised the proud paean, making glad my heart.
And I believed that Phoebus’ mouth divine,
Filled with the breath of prophecy, could not lie.
But he himself, the singer, himself who sat
At meat with us, himself who promised all,
Is now himself the slayer of my son. ’

chinese:
谁这样谈论诸神，我们就要对他发怒，拒绝为他提供歌舞队，也不让教师用他的作品教育年轻人。如果我们的护卫者要敬畏诸神，并在人类可能达到的范围内接近神，就必须如此。”
“正是，”他说，“我接受这些规范，愿把它们作为准则和法律来使用。”
english: When anyone says that sort of thing about the gods, we shall be wroth with him, we will refuse him a chorus, neither will we allow teachers to use him for the education of the young if our guardians are to be god-fearing men and god-like in so far as that is possible for humanity.” “By all means,” he said, “I accept these norms and would use them as canons and laws.”

chinese:
第三卷
苏格拉底：我说：“那么，关于诸神，如果我们要使孩子长大后敬重诸神、父亲和母亲，不轻视彼此的友谊，这便是从小应当准许或不准许他们听到的故事。”
“这是我们的看法，我也认为是对的。”
“那么再看这一点：如果要使他们勇敢，我们的规定难道不也必须包括那些最能使他们不怕死的言辞吗？
english: “Concerning the gods then,” said I, “this is the sort of thing that we must allow or not allow them to hear from childhood up, if they are to honor the gods and their fathers and mothers, and not to hold their friendship with one another in light esteem.” “That was our view and I believe it right.” “What then of this? If they are to be brave, must we not extend our prescription to include also the sayings that will make them least likely to fear death?

chinese:
你难道认为，一个心里怀着这种恐惧的人，能成为勇敢的人吗？”
“不，我确实不这样认为。”他回答。
“再说，假如一个人相信冥府和那里的恐怖确实存在，你认为他能不怕死，在战斗中宁愿死去也不愿战败而沦为奴隶吗？”
“绝不可能。”
“那么看来，我们也必须监督那些负责讲述这类故事的人，请他们不要这样不加分别地贬斥冥府中的生活，而应当赞美它；
english: Or do you suppose that anyone could ever become brave who had that dread in his heart?” “No indeed, I do not,” he replied. “And again if he believes in the reality of the underworld and its terrors, do you think that any man will be fearless of death and in battle will prefer death to defeat and slavery?” “By no means.” “Then it seems we must exercise supervision also, in the matter of such tales as these, over those who undertake to supply them and request them not to dispraise in this undiscriminating fashion the life in Hades but rather praise it,

chinese:
因为他们现在讲的，既不真实，也无益于将来要成为战士的人。”
“是的，必须这样。”他说。
“那么，”我说，“我们就从下面这几句开始，把同类的诗句统统删去：
‘我宁愿在人间的田地里替别人做雇工，
替一个仅有薄田、所得不足糊口的人耕种，
也不愿统治所有已经死去的亡者，做他们的王。’
还有这几句：
english:
since what they now tell us is neither true nor edifying to men who are destined to be warriors.” “Yes, we must,” he said. “Then,” said I, “beginning with this verse we will expunge everything of the same kind: ‘
Liefer were I in the fields up above to be serf to another
Tiller of some poor plot which yields him a scanty subsistence,
Than to be ruler and king over all the dead who have perished,’ and this: ‘

chinese:
‘免得死者的居所向凡人和诸神敞露，
那阴森、恶臭、潮湿的地方，连诸神也憎恶。’
还有：
‘唉！原来即使在冥府的居所，
也还有灵魂和幻影，只是其中全无知觉。’
还有：
‘唯独他仍有智慧和心智，其余都只是飘忽的阴影。’
还有：
‘他的灵魂不情愿地离开肢体，飞往冥府，
哀叹自己的命运、失去的强健和盛年的青春。’
english:
Lest unto men and immortals the homes of the dead be uncovered
Horrible, noisome, dank, that the gods too hold in abhorrence, ’ and: ‘
Ah me! so it is true that e’en in the dwellings of Hades
Spirit there is and wraith, but within there is no understanding,’ and this: ‘
Sole to have wisdom and wit, but the others are shadowy phantoms,’ and: ‘
Forth from his limbs unwilling his spirit flitted to Hades,
Wailing its doom and its lustihood lost and the May of its manhood,’ ”

chinese:
还有：
‘那啾啾鸣叫的灵魂，像烟一样消失在地下。’
还有：
‘正如蝙蝠在幽深的洞穴里，
当一只从聚成一团的蝙蝠中坠落，
便尖叫着飞起——它们攀着岩石，一只紧挨着一只——
那些鬼魂也这样啾啾鸣叫着飞去。’
english:
and:‘
Under the earth like a vapor vanished the gibbering soul, ’ and: ‘
Even as bats in the hollow of some mysterious grotto
Fly with a flittermouse shriek when one of them falls from the cluster
Whereby they hold to the rock and are clinging the one to the other,
Flitted their gibbering ghosts. ’

chinese:
我们要请荷马和其他诗人不要生气，因为我们删去这些诗句和一切类似的段落，并不是说它们没有诗意，也不是说大多数听众不喜欢，而是因为它们越富于诗意，就越不适合让那些将成为自由人、畏惧奴役甚于死亡的孩子和成人听见。”
“完全如此。”
“那么，在这些事情上，我们还必须进一步禁止所有引起恐怖和畏惧的名称：以高声哀哭
english:
We will beg Homer and the other poets not to be angry if we cancel those and all similar passages, not that they are not poetic and pleasing to most hearers, but because the more poetic they are the less are they suited to the ears of boys and men who are destined to be free and to be more afraid of slavery than of death.” “By all means.”

“Then we must further taboo in these matters the entire vocabulary of terror and fear, Cocytus

chinese:
得名的科库托斯河、可憎的斯堤克斯河——那流淌致命仇恨的河流——地狱深坑和坟窟中的居民，以及一切同类的说法；单是这些名称，每次就能使听众浑身战栗。这些说法用于别的目的，也许十分出色；但我们担心，护卫者习惯了这种惊惧，就会比我们希望的更加敏感、软弱。”
“这样的担心是对的。”
“那么，必须把这些除去？”
“是的。”
“无论散文还是诗歌，我们都必须要求与之相反的说法？”
“显然如此。”
“我们是不是也要除去
english: named of lamentation loud, abhorred Styx, the flood of deadly hate, the people of the infernal pit and of the charnel-house, and all other terms of this type, whose very names send a shudder through all the hearers every year. And they may be excellent for other purposes, but we are in fear for our guardians lest the habit of such thrills make them more sensitive and soft than we would have them.” “And we are right in so fearing.” “We must remove those things then?” “Yes.” “And the opposite type to them is what we must require in speech and in verse?” “Obviously.” “And shall we also do away with the

chinese:
那些有名望的人的哭号和哀叹？”
“从前面的结论看，”他说，“这是必然的。”
“想想看，”我说，“我们这样除去它们，究竟对不对。我们主张，一个好人不会认为另一个好人的死是可怕的事，即使死者是他的朋友。”
“是的，我们这样说。”
“那么，他就不会仿佛朋友遭到了什么可怕的祸患，而为朋友哀哭。”
“当然不会。”
“但我们还说，这样的人在所有人中，最能依靠自己
english: wailings and lamentations of men of repute?” “That necessarily follows,” he said, “from the other.” “Consider,” said I, “whether we shall be right in thus getting rid of them or not. What we affirm is that a good man will not think that for a good man, whose friend he also is, death is a terrible thing.” “Yes, we say that.” “Then it would not be for his friend’s sake as if he had suffered something dreadful that he would make lament.” “Certainly not.” “But we also say this, that such a one is most of all men sufficient unto himself

chinese:
过上良好的生活；他与别人不同，最少需要任何其他人。”
“对。”他回答。
“那么，失去儿子、兄弟、财产或任何类似的东西，对他来说，也最不会是可怕的事。”
“最不会。”
“因此，当这样的不幸降临到他身上，他的哀哭最少，也最能有节制地承受。”
“当然。”
“那么，我们除去有名望的人的哀哭，把这些归给女人，
english:
for a good life and is distinguished from other men in having least need of anybody else.” “True,” he replied. “Least of all then to him is it a terrible thing to lose son or brother or his wealth or anything of the sort.” “Least of all.” “Then he makes the least lament and bears it most moderately when any such misfortune overtakes him.” “Certainly.”

“Then we should be right in doing away with the lamentations of men of note and in attributing them to women,

chinese:
而且还不是女人中最出色的那些，并且归给卑劣的男人，使我们说要培养来保卫国土的人鄙视这样的行为，就是对的。”
“是对的。”他说。
“那么，我们还要请求荷马和其他诗人，不要把女神之子阿喀琉斯描绘成这样：
‘时而侧卧，时而又仰卧，
时而又俯伏着躺下。’
然后起身，
‘心神狂乱地徘徊在荒凉、不生庄稼的海岸。’
english:
and not to the most worthy of them either, and to inferior men, in that those whom we say we are breeding for the guardianship of the land may disdain to act like these.” “We should be right,” said he. “Again then we shall request Homer and the other poets not to portray Achilles, the son of a goddess, as,‘
Lying now on his side, and then again on his back,
And again on his face,’ and then rising up and ‘Drifting distraught on the shore of the waste unharvested ocean,’

chinese:
也不要写他‘双手抓起乌黑的尘土，撒在头上’，或写他像诗人所描绘的那样无休无止地哭泣哀号；也不要写与诸神亲缘相近的普里阿摩斯，在粪土中翻滚着恳求：
‘向每个人高声呼喊，一个个叫着他们的名字。’
更进一步，我们尤其要请求他们，不要把诸神描绘成哀叹哭号的样子，说：
english:
nor ‘“clutching with both hands the sooty dust and strewing it over his head,”’ nor as weeping and lamenting in the measure and manner attributed to him by the poet; nor yet Priam, near kinsman of the gods, making supplication and rolling in the dung, ‘
Calling aloud unto each, by name to each man appealing. ’ And yet more than this shall we beg of them at least not to describe the gods as lamenting and crying, ‘

chinese:
‘啊，我多么不幸！我这可怜的母亲，生下最英勇的儿子，却给自己带来悲伤！’
即便他们要这样描写诸神，至少也不要竟敢把至高的神写成如此不可信的模样，让他说：
‘唉！那人如此为我所爱，
我却眼看着他在特洛伊城边被追赶，心中满是悲伤！’
还有：
‘唉！在所有人中，萨尔佩冬最为我所爱，
english:
Ah, woe is me, woeful mother who bore to my sorrow the bravest, ’ and if they will so picture the gods at least not to have the effrontery to present so unlikely a likeness of the supreme god as to make him say:‘
Out on it, dear to my heart is the man whose pursuit around Troy-town
I must behold with my eyes while my spirit is grieving within me, ’ and: ‘
Ah, woe is me! of all men to me is Sarpedon the dearest,’ ‘

chinese:
却命定要死在墨诺提俄斯之子帕特罗克洛斯手下。’
“因为，亲爱的阿德曼托斯，如果我们的年轻人认真听信这些故事，而不把它们当作不配如此人物的言辞来嘲笑，那么，当他们自己想要做出或说出这类事情时，就更不会认为有失身份，也不会责备自己；他们反而会毫无羞耻、毫无节制地，为一点小事唱出许多哀歌，发出许多悲叹。”
english:
Fated to fall by the hands of Patroclus, Menoitius’ offspring.’

For if, dear Adeimantus, our young men should seriously incline to listen to such tales and not laugh at them as unworthy utterances, still less surely would any man be to think such conduct unworthy of himself and to rebuke himself if it occurred to him to do or say anything of that kind, but without shame or restraint full many a dirge for trifles would he chant and many a lament.”

chinese:
“你说得完全正确。”他回答。
“可是，正如我们刚才的论证所表明的，这种情形决不能发生。除非有人用更好的理由使我们信服，否则我们必须相信这番论证。”
“是的，决不能。”
“再说，他们也不应当动辄大笑。因为通常一个人任自己狂笑不止，这样的状态会引发剧烈的反转。”
“我也这么想。”他说。
“那么，如果有人把有价值的人描写成被
english:
“You say most truly,” he replied. “But that must not be, as our reasoning but now showed us, in which we must put our trust until someone convinces with a better reason.” “No, it must not be.” “Again, they must not be prone to laughter. For ordinarily when one abandons himself to violent laughter his condition provokes a violent reaction.” “I think so,” he said.

“Then if anyone represents men of worth as overpowered

chinese:
大笑支配的样子，我们不能接受；若这样描写诸神，就更不能接受。”
“当然更不能。”他回答。
“那么，荷马关于诸神的这些诗句，我们也不能接受：
‘有福的诸神看见赫淮斯托斯忙着侍奉，喘着粗气，
便爆发出止也止不住的笑声。’
照你的看法，我们不能接受这种描写。”
english:
by laughter we must accept it, much less if gods.” “Much indeed,” he replied. “Then we must not accept from Homer such sayings as these either about the gods:‘
Quenchless then was the laughter that rose from the blessed immortals
When they beheld Hephaestus officiously puffing and panting.’ — we must not accept it on your view.”

chinese:
“如果你愿意说是我的看法，”他说，“那么就算是吧；总之，我们不能接受。”
“此外，我们当然必须把真实看得极其珍贵。假如我们刚才说得对，虚假对于诸神确实毫无用处，对于人却可以像药物一样有所裨益，那么显然，这种东西必须交给医生使用，外行人不应碰它。”
“显然如此。”他回答。
“那么，城邦中若有人可以适当地说谎，那应当是统治者：他们可以为了城邦的利益，在涉及敌人或公民的事情上说谎；其他人一概不得这样做。
english: “If it pleases you to call it mine,” he said; “at any rate we must not accept it.” “But further we must surely prize truth most highly. For if we were right in what we were just saying and falsehood is in very deed useless to gods, but to men useful as a remedy or form of medicine, it is obvious that such a thing must be assigned to physicians and laymen should have nothing to do with it.” “Obviously,” he replied. “The rulers then of the city may, if anybody, fitly lie on account of enemies or citizens for the benefit of the state; no others may have anything to do with it,

chinese:
但是，如果普通人向这样的统治者说谎，我们就要说，这罪过至少同病人不向医生、运动员不向教练如实交代自己的身体状况一样大，甚至更大；也同一个人就船只和船员的事情欺骗舵手，隐瞒自己或同船伙伴的真实状况以及他们的遭遇一样大。”
“完全正确。”他回答。
“那么，如果
english: but for a layman to lie to rulers of that kind we shall affirm to be as great a sin, nay a greater, than it is for a patient not to tell physician or an athlete his trainer the truth about his bodily condition, or for a man to deceive the pilot about the ship and the sailors as to the real condition of himself or a fellow-sailor, and how they fare.” “Most true,” he replied. “If then

chinese:
统治者抓到城邦里其他人说谎，无论他是哪一种工匠——
‘无论是预言者、治病的人，还是木匠’——
他都会惩罚这个人，因为他引入的这种做法，足以颠覆、毁坏一个城邦，正如它足以毁坏一条船一样。”
“如果言行一致，”他说，“就会这样。”
“再说，我们的年轻人难道不需要节制这种德性吗？”
“当然需要。”
“对于大多数人，节制的要点不就是这些：服从他们的统治者，并由自己统治
english:
the ruler catches anybody else in the city lying, any of the craftsmen ‘
Whether a prophet or healer of sickness or joiner of timbers,’ he will chastise him for introducing a practice as subversive and destructive of a state as it is of a ship.” “He will,” he said, “if deed follows upon word.” “Again, will our lads not need the virtue of self-control?” “Of course.” “And for the multitude are not the main points of self-control these—to be obedient to their rulers and themselves to be rulers

chinese:
身体的欲望，以及饮食和其他方面的快乐吗？”
“我认为是的。”
“那么，我想，我们会认为荷马笔下狄俄墨得斯这样的言辞说得好：
‘朋友，坐下，保持安静，听从我的吩咐。’
还有下面的诗句：
‘阿开奥人精神昂扬，却默默行进，因为敬畏自己的统帅。’
以及所有同类的段落。”
english:
over the bodily appetites and pleasures of food, drink, and the rest?” “I think so.” “Then, I take it, we will think well said such sayings as that of Homer’s Diomede:‘
Friend, sit down and be silent and hark to the word of my bidding, ’ and what follows:‘
Breathing high spirit the Greeks marched silently fearing their captains, ’ and all similar passages.”

chinese:
“是的，说得好。”
“那么，这样的说法又怎样：
‘醉醺醺的家伙，长着狗的眼睛、逃鹿的心！’
以及接下来的诗句，这些说得好吗？还有普通公民对统治者说的其他傲慢无礼的话，无论散文还是诗歌，都好吗？”
“不好。”
“它们当然不适合让年轻人听来培养节制。不过，从另一个角度看，它们若能给人一点乐趣，我们也不必奇怪。你的看法怎样？”
“和你一样。”他说。
“再说，把最有智慧的人写成这样说：在他看来，世间最美好的事情就是——
‘当丰盛的餐桌已经摆好，
english:
“Yes, well said.” “But what of this sort of thing? ‘
Heavy with wine with the eyes of a dog and the heart of a fleet deer,’ and the lines that follow, are these well—and other impertinences in prose or verse of private citizens to their rulers?” “They are not well.” “They certainly are not suitable for youth to hear for the inculcation of self-control. But if from another point of view they yield some pleasure we must not be surprised, or what is your view of it?” “This,” he said.

“Again, to represent the wisest man as saying that this seems to him the fairest thing in the world, ‘
When the bounteous tables are standing

chinese:
上面堆满面包和肉，侍酒者从调酒缸中舀起甜酒，
端来倒进每个人的杯子。’
你认为，年轻人听了这些，有助于养成节制、自持吗？还有这一句：
‘饥饿是凡人所能遭受的最悲惨的死法。’
或者，让他们听说宙斯由于欲望激动，轻易就忘记了自己趁其他诸神睡着、独自醒着时所拟定的全部计划，
english:
Laden with bread and with meat and the cupbearer ladles the sweet wine
Out of the mixer and bears it and empties it into the beakers. ’ —do you think the hearing of that sort of thing will conduce to a young man’s temperance or self-control? or this:‘
Hunger is the most piteous death that a mortal may suffer.’ Or to hear how Zeus lightly forgot all the designs which he devised,

chinese:
看见赫拉便不能自持，甚至不愿去他们的寝室，却想就在地上与她交合，还说自己欲火之盛，胜过他们最初
‘瞒着亲爱的双亲’
彼此结合的时候。让他们听说赫淮斯托斯因为同类的事情把阿瑞斯和阿佛洛狄忒锁在一起，也不会对他们有益。”
“是的，凭宙斯起誓，”他说，
english: watching while the other gods slept, because of the excitement of his passions, and was so overcome by the sight of Hera that he is not even willing to go to their chamber, but wants to lie with her there on the ground and says that he is possessed by a fiercer desire than when they first consorted with one another, ‘Deceiving their dear parents.’ Nor will it profit them to hear of Hephaestus’s fettering Ares and Aphrodite for a like motive.” “No, by Zeus,” he said,

chinese:
“我不认为这会有益。”
“但是，凡是表现有名望的人在一切逆境面前坚忍不屈的言行，都适合呈现给我们的年轻人看，也适合讲给他们听。例如：
‘他捶着胸膛，这样责备自己的心：
忍耐吧，我的心；你曾经忍受过更坏的事。’”
“完全如此。”他说。
“有一点是确定的：我们不能让我们的人接受贿赂、贪求利益。”
english:
“I don’t think it will.” “But any words or deeds of endurance in the face of all odds attributed to famous men are suitable for our youth to see represented and to hear, such as:‘
He smote his breast and chided thus his heart,
“Endure, my heart, for worse hast thou endured.”’ ” “By all means,” he said. “It is certain that we cannot allow our men to be acceptors of bribes or greedy for gain.”

chinese:
“绝对不能。”
“那么，他们不得吟唱：‘礼物能打动诸神，礼物能说服可畏的君王。’我们也不应赞许阿喀琉斯的随从福尼克斯，说他劝阿喀琉斯的话很妥当——他劝阿喀琉斯，若能得到礼物就去保卫阿开奥人，若没有礼物就不要息怒。我们也不应认为阿喀琉斯如此贪婪是合宜的，或承认他确实如此：收下阿伽门农的礼物，又在得到赎金后交还一具尸体，否则就不肯交还。”
english:
“By no means.” “Then they must not chant: ‘
Gifts move the gods and gifts persuade dread kings.’ Nor should we approve Achilles’ attendant Phoenix as speaking fairly when he counselled him if he received gifts for it to defend the Achaeans, but without gifts not to lay aside his wrath;”

nor shall we think it proper nor admit that Achilles himself was so greedy as to accept gifts from Agamemnon and again to give up a dead body after receiving payment but otherwise to refuse.”

chinese:
“称赞这样的行为，”他说，“是不对的。”
“可是，出于对荷马的顾惜，”我说，“我还不愿直说：断言阿喀琉斯做过这些事，或听别人这么说便相信，实在是不敬神；相信他曾对阿波罗说下面的话，也是如此：
‘远射之神，你骗了我，你是所有神中最可恶的！
要是我的双手有这能力，我一定狠狠报复你。’
english:
“It is not right,” he said, “to commend such conduct.” “But, for Homer’s sake,” said I, “I hesitate to say that it is positively impious to affirm such things of Achilles and to believe them when told by others; or again to believe that he said to Apollo ‘
Me thou hast baulked, Far-darter, the most pernicious of all gods,
Mightily would I requite thee if only my hands had the power. ’

chinese:
还有，说他不服从那位身为神祇的河神，甚至准备与之搏斗；又说他曾就自己奉献给斯佩耳刻俄斯河的头发说：
‘就让我把这头发交给英雄帕特罗克洛斯，让他带走吧。’
而帕特罗克洛斯已经是一具尸体；他们还要我们相信，他确实这样做了。此外，他把赫克托耳的尸体拖着绕帕特罗克洛斯的坟墓行走，又在他的火葬堆上宰杀活着的俘虏：这一切，我们都要断言是虚假的。
english: And how he was disobedient to the river, who was a god and was ready to fight with him, and again that he said of the locks of his hair, consecrated to her river Spercheius: ‘This let me give to take with him my hair to the hero, Patroclus,’ who was a dead body, and that he did so we must believe. And again the trailings of Hector’s body round the grave of Patroclus and the slaughter of the living captives upon his pyre, all these we will affirm to be lies,

chinese:
我们也决不允许年轻人相信，阿喀琉斯——女神与最贞洁的珀琉斯之子、宙斯的后裔，又亲自在最有智慧的喀戎照料下长大——竟然心性如此紊乱，同时染上两种彼此矛盾的疾病：一种是不配自由人的贪婪，另一种是对神与人都狂妄无礼的傲慢。”
“你说得对。”他说。
“那么，”我说，“我们既不能相信，也不能容许别人说：波塞冬之子忒修斯
english:
nor will we suffer our youth to believe that Achilles, the son of a goddess and of Peleus the most chaste of men, grandson of Zeus, and himself bred under the care of the most sage Cheiron, was of so perturbed a spirit as to be affected with two contradictory maladies, the greed that becomes no free man and at the same time overweening arrogance towards gods and men.” “You are right,” he said.

“Neither, then,” said I, “must we believe this or suffer it to be said, that Theseus, the son of Poseidon,

chinese: 和宙斯之子佩里托俄斯曾经企图进行那些骇人的劫夺妇女之事；或说任何别的神之子和英雄，竟肯去做现在那些人妄称他做过的可怕而不敬神的事情。我们必须要求诗人二择其一：要么否认这些事是他们做的，要么否认他们是诸神的子女；决不能两者并说，也不能企图使年轻人相信，诸神是恶的生育者，英雄也并不比常人更好。
english: and Peirithous, the son of Zeus, attempted such dreadful rapes, nor that any other child of a god and hero would have brought himself to accomplish the terrible and impious deeds that they now falsely relate of him. But we must constrain the poets either to deny that these are their deeds or that they are the children of gods, but not to make both statements or attempt to persuade our youth that the gods are the begetters of evil, and that heroes are no better than men.

chinese:
因为，正如我们刚才说的，这些言辞既不敬神，又是虚假的。我想，我们已经证明，恶是不可能来自诸神的。”
“当然。”
“而且，它们对听者还有害。一个人如果确信，这样的行为正是下列那些人现在和过去所做的，就会十分宽宥自己的恶行：
‘诸神亲播的种裔，
与宙斯血缘相近；在伊达山顶，
他们祖传祭坛的火焰升入最高的天空，
他们的血液里也从未熄灭神圣的火。’
因此，我们必须禁止这样的故事，以免它们使年轻人在丑恶之事上变得极其放纵。”
english:
For, as we were saying, such utterances are both impious and false. For we proved, I take it, that for evil to arise from gods is an impossibility.” “Certainly.” “And they are furthermore harmful to those that hear them. For every man will be very lenient with his own misdeeds if he is convinced that such are and were the actions of ‘
The near-sown seed of gods,
Close kin to Zeus, for whom on Ida’s top
Ancestral altars flame to highest heaven,
Nor in their life-blood fails the fire divine.’ ”

For which cause we must put down such fables, lest they breed in our youth great laxity in turpitude.”

chinese:
“确实必须如此。”
“还有哪一类言辞，需要我们规定准许什么、禁止什么？”
“关于诸神、精灵、英雄和冥府，我们已经说明该怎样讲述。”
“是的。”
“那么，剩下的就是关于人的言辞。”
“显然如此。”
“朋友，这一类我们现在还不能放在这里处理。”
“为什么？”
“因为，我想，我们将要说，诗人
english: “Most assuredly.” “What type of discourse remains for our definition of our prescriptions and proscriptions?” “We have declared the right way of speaking about gods and daemons and heroes and that other world.” “We have.” “Speech, then, about men would be the remainder.” “Obviously.” “It is impossible for us, my friend, to place this here.” “Why?” “Because I presume we are going to say that so it is that both poets

chinese:
和散文作者在最重大的事情上，对人的说法都是错误的：他们说，有许多人虽然不正义却幸福，许多正义的人却悲惨；又说，只要能隐瞒，不正义便能获利，正义则是别人的好处、自己的损失。我想，我们将禁止他们这样说，并命令他们在诗歌和故事中讲相反的事情。你不这样认为吗？”
“不止认为，”他说，“我很清楚必定如此。”
“那么，如果你承认我说得对，我是不是就可以说，你已经让步，承认了我们最初所研究的那个论点？”
english: and writers of prose speak wrongly about men in matters of greatest moment, saying that there are many examples of men who, though unjust, are happy, and of just men who are wretched, and that there is profit in injustice if it be concealed, and that justice is the other man’s good and your own loss; and I presume that we shall forbid them to say this sort of thing and command them to sing and fable the opposite. Don’t you think so?” “Nay, I well know it,” he said. “Then, if you admit that I am right, I will say that you have conceded the original point of our inquiry?”

chinese:
“你理解得对。”他说。
“那么，关于人的言辞应当如此这一点，等到我们发现正义的本性，并证明无论一个人看起来正义与否，正义都对拥有它的人有利之后，再来取得一致。”
“完全正确。”他回答。
“这样，故事的内容就谈完了。我想，接下来应当考察表达的方式。这样我们就把说什么与怎样说都考察完全了。”
阿德曼托斯说：“我不明白你这话的意思。”
english:
“Rightly apprehended,” he said. “Then, as regards men that speech must be of this kind, that is a point that we will agree upon when we have discovered the nature of justice and the proof that it is profitable to its possessor whether he does or does not appear to be just.” “Most true,” he replied.

“So this concludes the topic of tales. That of diction, I take it, is to be considered next. So we shall have completely examined both the matter and the manner of speech.” And Adeimantus said, “I don’t understand what you mean by this.”

chinese:
“那么，”我说，“我们得让你明白。这样讲，你也许更容易理解：讲故事的人或诗人所说的一切，不都是叙述过去、现在或将来的事情吗？”
“还能是什么呢？”他说。
“他们不都是采用单纯叙述，或通过模仿来叙述，或两者兼用吗？”
“这一点，”他说，“我还是需要你讲得更清楚些。”
“看来我是个可笑而又含糊的老师，”我说，“那么，我就像那些不善表达的人一样，
english: “Well,” said I, “we must have you understand. Perhaps you will be more likely to apprehend it thus. Is not everything that is said by fabulists or poets a narration of past, present, or future things?” “What else could it be?” he said. “Do not they proceed either by pure narration or by a narrative that is effected through imitation, or by both?” “This too,” he said, “I still need to have made plainer.” “I seem to be a ridiculous and obscure teacher,” I said; “so like men who are unable to express themselves

chinese: 不再试着用总体的、普遍的说法，而取出一个具体部分，用这个例子来说明我的意思。告诉我，你知道《伊利亚特》开头那几行吗？诗人在那里说，克律塞斯恳求阿伽门农释放自己的女儿，国王却发怒了；克律塞斯
english:
I won’t try to speak in wholes and universals but will separate off a particular part and by the example of that try to show you my meaning.”

Tell me. Do you know the first lines if the Iliad in which the poet says that Chryses implored Agamemnon to release his daughter, and that the king was angry and that Chryses,

chinese:
请求不成，便向神祈祷，诅咒阿开奥人。”
“我知道。”
“那么你知道，直到下面这些诗句为止——
‘他恳求所有的阿开奥人，
尤其恳求阿特柔斯的两个儿子，那两位统率众人的领袖’——
都是诗人自己在说话，他丝毫没有试图让我们觉得，说话的是他以外的什么人。
english:
failing of his request, imprecated curses on the Achaeans in his prayers to the god?” “I do.” “You know then that as far as these verses,‘
And prayed unto all the Achaeans,
Chiefly to Atreus’ sons, twin leaders who marshalled the people, ’ the poet himself is the speaker and does not even attempt to suggest to us that anyone but himself is speaking.

chinese:
但接下来的话，他说得仿佛自己就是克律塞斯，尽可能让我们觉得，说话的不是荷马，而是那位年老的祭司。他叙述伊利昂的事情、伊塔卡发生的一切，以及整部《奥德赛》的其余部分，几乎都采用了这种方式。”
“正是如此。”他说。
“那么，无论他呈现各个人物的话，还是话语之间的事情，都属于叙述，不是吗？”
“当然。”
“但当他讲出一段话，
english: But what follows he delivers as if he were himself Chryses and tries as far as may be to make us feel that not Homer is the speaker, but the priest, an old man. And in this manner he has carried in nearly all the rest of his narration about affairs in Ilion, all that happened in Ithaca, and the entire Odyssey.” “Quite so,” he said. “Now, it is narration, is it not, both when he presents the several speeches and the matter between the speeches?” “Of course.” “But when he delivers a speech

chinese:
仿佛自己是另一个人时，我们是不是要说：此时他在尽可能让自己的说话方式接近他所宣布即将开口的那个人？”
“显然要这样说。”
“在言语或身体举止上使自己像另一个人，不就是模仿那个人吗？”
“当然。”
“那么在这种情形下，看来他和其他诗人都是通过模仿来进行叙述。”
“当然。”
“但如果诗人从不隐去自己，那么他的全部诗作和叙述，就都不经过模仿而完成了。
english: as if he were someone else, shall we not say that he then assimilates thereby his own diction is far as possible to that of the person whom he announces as about to speak?” “We shall obviously.” “And is not likening one’s self to another speech or bodily bearing an imitation of him to whom one likens one’s self?” “Surely.” “In such case then it appears he and the other poets effect their narration through imitation.” “Certainly.” “But if the poet should conceal himself nowhere, then his entire poetizing and narration would have been accomplished without imitation.

chinese: 为了免得你又说不明白，我就给你解释，这样做会是什么样子。如果荷马讲了克律塞斯带着女儿的赎金前来，向阿开奥人、尤其向他们的君王恳求以后，接着说话时仍然作为荷马，而不是装成或变成克律塞斯，那么你知道，这就不是模仿，而是单纯的叙述。它大致会是下面这个样子。因为我不是诗人，我就不用格律来说：
english: And lest you may say again that you don’t understand, I will explain to you how this would be done. If Homer, after telling us that Chryses came with the ransom of his daughter and as a suppliant of the Achaeans but chiefly of the kings, had gone on speaking not as if made or being Chryses but still as Homer, you are aware that it would not be imitation but narration, pure and simple. It would have been somewhat in this wise. I will state it without meter for I am not a poet:

chinese: 祭司前来，祈求诸神准许他们攻取特洛伊、平安返乡；同时请他们出于对神的敬畏，收下赎金，释放他的女儿。他这样说后，其他人心怀敬意，表示赞同，阿伽门农却发怒了，命令他离开，不许再来，否则，神的权杖和缎带也保护不了他。他说，他女儿在获释以前，会留在阿耳戈斯、在他身边衰老；又命令老人赶快走，不要再惹他生气，如果老人还想平安回家的话。
english:
the priest came and prayed that to them the gods should grant to take Troy and come safely home, but that they should accept the ransom and release his daughter, out of reverence for the god;”

and when he had thus spoken the others were of reverent mind and approved, but Agamemnon was angry and bade him depart and not come again lest the scepter and the fillets of the god should not avail him. And ere his daughter should be released, he said, she would grow old in Argos with himself, and he ordered him to be off and not vex him if he wished to get home safe.

chinese: 老人听了，心生恐惧，便默默离去。他走到离营地远些的地方，向阿波罗长久祈祷，呼唤神的各种称号，提醒神自己过去献上的礼物，并请求回报：无论是为神建造庙宇，还是献上祭牲，只要其中有任何一件曾讨神欢喜。他请求神用箭使阿开奥人为他的眼泪付出代价，以此回报这些奉献。亲爱的朋友，”我说，“这样，
english: And the old man on hearing this was frightened and departed in silence, and having gone apart from the camp he prayed at length to Apollo, invoking the appellations of the god, and reminding him of and asking requital for any of his gifts that had found favor whether in the building of temples or the sacrifice of victims. In return for these things he prayed that the Achaeans should suffer for his tears by the god’s shafts. It is in this way, my dear fellow,” I said, “that

chinese:
便成了没有模仿的单纯叙述。”
“我明白了。”他说。
“那么，”我说，“你也要明白，与之相反的方式，就是除去中间诗人自己说的话，只留下人物相互接续的话语。”
“这个我也明白，”他说，“悲剧就是这样。”
“你领会得非常准确，”我说，“现在我想，我能把先前没能讲清楚的事说明白了：有一类诗歌和故事，完全通过模仿来进行，
english:
without imitation simple narration results.” “I understand,” he said.

“Understand then,” said I, “that the opposite of this arises when one removes the words of the poet between and leaves the alternation of speeches.” “This too I understand,” he said, “—it is what happens in tragedy.” “You have conceived me most rightly,” I said, “and now I think I can make plain to you what I was unable to before, that there is one kind of poetry and tale-telling which works wholly through imitation,

chinese:
就是你提到的悲剧和喜剧；另一类采用诗人本人的讲述，我想，酒神颂歌就是最鲜明的例子；还有一类兼用两者，史诗和许多别的作品就是如此，如果你明白我的话。”
“我现在明白你先前的意思了。”他说。
“那么，也请回想前面说过的话：我们已经谈完了言辞的‘说什么’，还要考察它的‘怎样说’。”
“我记得。”
english: as you remarked, tragedy and comedy; and another which employs the recital of the poet himself, best exemplified, I presume, in the dithyramb; and there is again that which employs both, in epic poetry and in many other places, if you apprehend me.” “I understand now,” he said, “what you then meant.” “Recall then also the preceding statement that we were done with the ‘what’ of speech and still had to consider the ’how.’” “I remember.”

chinese:
“我当时的意思正是：我们必须决定，是否允许诗人以模仿者的身份叙述，或一部分采用模仿、一部分不用模仿；若两者兼用，各自适合什么事情；还是完全不许他们模仿。”
“我猜，”他说，“你是在考虑，我们的城邦是否接纳悲剧和喜剧。”
“也许是，”我说，“也许还不止于此。因为我自己确实还不知道。不过，论证的风吹向哪里，我们就航向哪里。”
english: “What I meant then was just this, that we must reach a decision whether we are to suffer our poets to narrate as imitators or in part as imitators and in part not, and what sort of things in each case, or not allow them to imitate at all.” “I divine,” he said, “that you are considering whether we shall admit tragedy and comedy into our city or not.” “Perhaps,” said I, “and perhaps even more than that. For I certainly do not yet know myself, but whithersoever the wind, as it were, of the argument blows, there lies our course.”

chinese:
“说得好。”他回答。
“那么，阿德曼托斯，我们必须留意的是这一点：我们希望护卫者成为善于模仿的人吗？或者，这也由我们前面说的话推出来：每个人只能把一种职业做好，不能同时做好许多种；如果尝试后一种做法，涉猎多端，就会哪一种也不出色？”
“当然可以这样推出来。”
“同样的原则不也适用于模仿吗？同一个人不能像模仿一种事情那样，把许多事情都模仿得好。”
“是的，不能。”
“那么，他就更加不能一面
english:
“Well said,” he replied. “This then, Adeimantus, is the point we must keep in view, do we wish our guardians to be good mimics or not? Or is this also a consequence of what we said before, that each one could practise well only one pursuit and not many, but if he attempted the latter, dabbling in many things, he would fail of distinction in all?” “Of course it is.” “And does not the same rule hold for imitation, that the same man is not able to imitate many things well as he can one?” “No, he is not.”

“Still less, then, will he be able to combine

chinese:
从事某种有价值的职业，一面模仿许多事情，成为多才的模仿者；因为，若我没有弄错，即使看来最相近的两种模仿，例如写悲剧和写喜剧，同一些人也不能同时把两者做好。你刚才不是把这两种都叫作模仿吗？”
“是的。而你说同一些人不能在两者上都成功，说得对；同样，一个人也不能既是优秀的吟诵者，又是优秀的演员。”
“对。”
“而且，
english: the practice of any worthy pursuit with the imitation of many things and the quality of a mimic; since, unless I mistake, the same men cannot practise well at once even the two forms of imitation that appear most nearly akin, as the writing of tragedy and comedy? Did you not just now call these two imitations?” “I did, and you are right in saying that the same men are not able to succeed in both, nor yet to be at once good rhapsodists and actors.” “True.” “But

chinese:
同一些人也不能既演悲剧，又演喜剧——这些不都是模仿吗？”
“是的，都是模仿。”
“在我看来，阿德曼托斯，人的能力还被分割成比这些更细小的份额，因此，人既不能模仿许多事情，也不能亲自做许多事情——模仿正是这些事情的摹本。”
“完全正确。”他回答。
“那么，如果我们坚持最初的原则：护卫者应当摆脱其他一切技艺，
english:
neither can the same men be actors for tragedies and comedies—and all these are imitations, are they not?” “Yes, imitations.” “And to still smaller coinage than this, in my opinion, Adeimantus, proceeds the fractioning of human faculty, so as to be incapable of imitating many things or of doing the things themselves of which the imitations are likenesses.” “Most true,” he replied.

“If, then, we are to maintain our original principle, that our guardians, released from all other crafts,

chinese: 成为维护城邦自由的专门匠人，除了有助于这一目的的事情，其他什么都不追求，那么，他们去做或模仿任何别的事情，都是不合适的。若要模仿，他们就应当从小模仿适合自己的榜样：勇敢、节制、虔敬、自由的人，以及其他这一类品质。凡不配自由人的事情，他们既不应去做，也不应善于模仿；其他任何可耻的事情也一样，以免他们从模仿
english: are to be expert craftsmen of civic liberty, and pursue nothing else that does not conduce to this, it would not be fitting for these to do nor yet to imitate anything else. But if they imitate they should from childhood up imitate what is appropriate to them—men, that is, who are brave, sober, pious, free and all things of that kind; but things unbecoming the free man they should neither do nor be clever at imitating, nor yet any other shameful thing, lest from the imitation

chinese:
之中染上实在的品性。你难道没有发现，模仿若从年轻时起一直持续到后来，就会在身体、言语和思想上沉淀为习惯，成为第二天性吗？”
“确实发现了。”他说。
“那么，我们所培养的这些人，我们希望他们成为好人，既然是男子，就不许他们扮演女人，模仿年轻或年老的女人同丈夫争吵、藐视上天、高声自夸、自以为幸福，或陷于不幸，
english: they imbibe the reality. Or have you not observed that imitations, if continued from youth far into life, settle down into habits and (second) nature in the body, the speech, and the thought?” “Yes, indeed,” said he. “We will not then allow our charges, whom we expect to prove good men, being men, to play the parts of women and imitate a woman young or old wrangling with her husband, defying heaven, loudly boasting, fortunate in her own conceit, or involved in misfortune

chinese:
满怀悲伤、哭泣哀号；更不许他们模仿生病、恋爱或分娩中的女人。”
“当然不许。”他回答。
“他们也不能模仿男女奴隶做奴隶的工作。”
“是的，这也不许。”
“看来，也不能模仿那些懦弱的坏人，他们的行为与我们刚才说的正好相反：彼此辱骂、相互讥刺，无论醉酒还是清醒，都说污言秽语，
english:
and possessed by grief and lamentation—still less a woman that is sick, in love, or in labor.” “Most certainly not,” he replied. “Nor may they imitate slaves, female and male, doing the offices of slaves.” “No, not that either.”

“Nor yet, as it seems, bad men who are cowards and who do the opposite of the things we just now spoke of, reviling and lampooning one another, speaking foul words in their cups or when sober

chinese:
并且像这样的人惯常所做的那样，在其他方面也以言语和行动伤害自己、伤害别人。我想，他们也不能养成在言语或行动上装作疯人的习惯。因为，虽然他们必须认识疯狂或邪恶的男女，却决不能做出或模仿任何这一类事情。”
“完全正确。”他说。
“那么这个呢？”我说，“他们要模仿铁匠和其他工匠，或三列桨战船上的桨手以及为他们喊节拍的人，或其他与这些相关的事情吗？”
english: and in other ways sinning against themselves and others in word and deed after the fashion of such men. And I take it they must not form the habit of likening themselves to madmen either in words nor yet in deeds. For while knowledge they must have both of mad and bad men and women, they must do and imitate nothing of this kind.” “Most true,” he said. “What of this?” I said, “—are they to imitate smiths and other craftsmen or the rowers of triremes and those who call the time to them or other things connected therewith?”

chinese:
“他们怎么会呢？”他说，“既然连留心这些事情都会被禁止。”
“那么，马的嘶鸣、牛的吼叫、河流的声响、海的咆哮、雷声，以及其他一切同类的声音——他们要模仿这些吗？”
“不，”他说，“他们已经被禁止发疯，也不许装作疯人。”
“那么，如果我理解了你的意思，”我说，“就有这样一种表达和叙述的形式，
english: “How could they,” he said, “since it will be forbidden them even to pay any attention to such things?” “Well, then, neighing horses and lowing bulls, and the noise of rivers and the roar of the sea and the thunder and everything of that kind—will they imitate these?” “Nay, they have been forbidden,” he said, “to be mad or liken themselves to madmen.” “If, then, I understand your meaning,” said I, “there is a form of diction and narrative in which

chinese:
真正善良正直的人会用它来讲述自己要说的一切；另有一种与之不同的形式，出身和教养相反的人会依从它，用它来讲自己的故事。”
“这两种形式是什么？”他说。
“我想，一个品性端正的人，在叙述中遇到好人的某种言语或行动，会愿意扮成那个人来报告，不会因这种模仿感到羞耻。他尤其乐于模仿好人
english: the really good and true man would narrate anything that he had to say, and another form unlike this to which the man of the opposite birth and breeding would cleave and which he would tell his story.” “What are these forms?” he said. “A man of the right sort, I think, when he comes in the course of his narrative to some word or act of a good man will be willing to impersonate the other in reporting it, and will feel no shame at that kind of mimicry, by preference imitating the good man

chinese: 坚定而明智的行动；若好人因疾病、爱情、醉酒或其他不幸而失去常态，他就会模仿得少些，也更不情愿。但当他遇到不如自己的人，除了那人偶尔做出好事的少数情形，他不愿认真地使自己像一个低于自己的人，而会觉得难为情：一来，他不熟悉对这种性格的模仿；二来，他厌恶把自己塑造成卑劣事物的样子，厌恶使自己去适应它们。
english: when he acts steadfastly and sensibly, and less and more reluctantly when he is upset by sickness or love or drunkenness or any other mishap. But when he comes to someone unworthy of himself, he will not wish to liken himself in earnest to one who is inferior, except in the few cases where he is doing something good, but will be embarrassed both because he is unpractised in the mimicry of such characters, and also because he shrinks in distaste from molding and fitting himself the types of baser things.

chinese:
除非是开玩笑，否则他的心灵鄙弃它们。”
“自然如此。”他说。
“那么，他采用的叙述，就是我们刚才用荷马诗句举例说明的那一种。他的表达会兼有模仿和单纯叙述，但在长篇言辞中，模仿只占很少一部分——我说的难道没有道理吗？”
“很有道理，”他说，“这种说话者的形式和样式正是如此。”
“那么，”我说，
english:
His mind disdains them, unless it be for jest.” “Naturally,” he said.

“Then the narrative that he will employ will be the kind that we just now illustrated by the verses of Homer, and his diction will be one that partakes of both, of imitation and simple narration, but there will be a small portion of imitation in a long discourse—or is there nothing in what I say?” “Yes, indeed,” he said, “that is the type and pattern of such a speaker.”

“Then,” said I,

chinese: “另一种说话者越是卑劣，就越不怕模仿任何事物。他会认为什么都不失自己的身份，因此会在许多人面前，认真地尝试模仿一切，包括我们刚才说的那些：雷鸣、风声、冰雹声、车轴和滑轮的声响，号角、管笛和排箫的音调，以及所有乐器的声音，还有狗、羊和鸟的叫声。这样，他的表达方式就会完全依靠
english: “the other kind speaker, the more debased he is the less will he shrink from imitating anything and everything. He will think nothing unworthy of himself, so that he will attempt, seriously and in the presence of many, to imitate all things, including those we just now mentioned—claps of thunder, and the noise of wind and hail and axles and pulleys, and the notes of trumpets and flutes and pan-pipes, and the sounds of all instruments, and the cries of dogs, sheep, and birds; and so his style will depend wholly on imitation

chinese:
声音和动作的模仿，或者只含有很少一点单纯叙述。”
“这也是必然的。”他说。
“那么，”我说，“这就是我所说的两种表达方式。”
“是有这两种。”他回答。
“其中一种所含的变化不是很少吗？如果我们给它配上合宜的音调和节奏，结果不就是：端正的说话者几乎用同一种音调、同一种抑扬来讲述——因为变化很少——
english: in voice and gesture, or will contain but a little of pure narration.” “That too follows of necessity,” he said. “These, then,” said I, “were the two types of diction of which I was aking.” “There are those two,” he replied. “Now does not one of the two involve slight variations, and if we assign a suitable pitch and rhythm to the diction, is not the result that the right speaker speaks almost on the same note and in one cadence—for the changes are slight—

chinese:
节奏也同样几乎始终是同一类吗？”
“正是如此。”
“那么，另一种呢？它如果也要得到适当的表达，难道不需要与此相反，采用每一种音调、所有的节奏吗？因为它包含许许多多不同的变化。”
“确实如此。”
“所有诗人和说话者，采用的不都是这两种表达方式之一，或是把两者组合起来的某种混合形式吗？”
english: and similarly in a rhythm of nearly the same kind?” “Quite so.” “But what of the other type? Does it not require the opposite, every kind of pitch and all rhythms, if it too is to have appropriate expression, since it involves manifold forms of variation?” “Emphatically so.” “And do all poets and speakers hit upon one type or the other of diction or some blend which they combine of both?”

chinese:
“必定如此。”他说。
“那么，”我说，“我们该怎么办？把这些方式全部引入城邦，还是只引入一种纯粹的方式，或引入混合的方式？”
“如果由我的一票决定，”他说，“我选只模仿好人的纯粹方式。”
“不过，阿德曼托斯，混合的方式也很讨人喜欢；而最讨孩子、他们的教师和广大民众喜欢的，恰恰是与你选择相反的那一种。”
“它确实最讨人喜欢。”
“但是，”我说，“也许你会断言，它不适合
english: “They must,” he said. “What, then,” said I, “are we to do? Shall we admit all of these into the city, or one of the unmixed types, or the mixed type?” “If my vote prevails,” he said, “the unmixed imitator of the good.” “Nay, but the mixed type also is pleasing, Adeimantus, and far most pleasing to boys and their tutors and the great mob is the opposite of your choice.” “Most pleasing it is.” “But perhaps,” said I, “you would affirm it to be ill-suited

chinese:
我们的政体，因为我们这里没有身兼两职或多职的人，每个人只做一件事。”
“它不适合。”
“这不也就是为什么，唯有在这样的城邦里，我们才会发现：鞋匠就是鞋匠，不在制鞋之外兼任舵手；农夫就是农夫，不在务农之外兼任法官；军人就是军人，不在当兵之外兼做生意；其他人也都是如此吗？”
“对。”他说。
“那么看来，如果有这样一个人，
english:
to our polity, because there is no twofold or manifold man among us, since every man does one thing.” “It is not suited.” “And is this not the reason why such a city is the only one in which we shall find the cobbler a cobbler and not a pilot in addition to his cobbling, and the farmer a farmer and not a judge added to his farming, and the soldier a soldier and not a money-maker in addition to his soldiery, and so of all the rest?” “True,” he said.

“If a man, then, it seems,

chinese: 凭借他的巧妙技艺，能够变换成各种形貌、模仿一切事物，带着想要展示的诗作来到我们的城邦，我们会伏地敬拜他，把他当作神圣、奇妙而令人愉悦的人物；但我们会对他说，我们城邦中没有这种人，也不允许产生这种人。然后，我们会把没药倒在他头上，给他戴上羊毛编成的饰带，请他到别的城邦去。而为了我们灵魂的益处，我们自己仍将采用
english: who was capable by his cunning of assuming every kind of shape and imitating all things should arrive in our city, bringing with himself the poems which he wished to exhibit, we should fall down and worship him as a holy and wondrous and delightful creature, but should say to him that there is no man of that kind among us in our city, nor is it lawful for such a man to arise among us, and we should send him away to another city, after pouring myrrh down over his head and crowning him with fillets of wool, but we ourselves, for our souls’ good, should continue to employ

chinese:
更严肃、较少令人愉悦的诗人和故事讲述者；他会模仿好人的表达方式，按照我们起初着手教育战士时规定的样式，来讲述自己的故事。”
“如果由我们作主，我们当然会这样做。”
“那么，朋友，”我说，“现在我们可以说，诗乐中涉及言辞和故事的部分，已经彻底完成了。因为我们已经规定了应当说什么，也规定了应当怎样说。”
“我也这样认为。”他回答。
english: the more austere and less delightful poet and tale-teller, who would imitate the diction of the good man and would tell his tale in the patterns which we prescribed in the beginning, when we set out to educate our soldiers.” “We certainly should do that if it rested with us.” “And now, my friend,” said I, “we may say that we have completely finished the part of music that concerns speeches and tales. For we have set forth what is to be said and how it is to be said.” “I think so too,” he replied.

chinese:
“那么，接下来，”我说，“就是歌曲和曲调的方式了？”
“显然如此。”
“既然已经讨论到这里，为了与前面所说的一致，我们该说它们具有怎样的性质，难道不是人人都能想出来吗？”
格劳孔笑着说：“恐怕这个‘人人’并不包括我。我虽有些猜想，却不能立刻充分推知我们该说什么。”
“我想，”我说，“至少这一点你一定
english: “After this, then,” said I, “comes the manner of song and tunes?” “Obviously.” “And having gone thus far, could not everybody discover what we must say of their character in order to conform to what has already been said?” “I am afraid that ‘everybody’ does not include me,” laughed Glaucon; “I cannot sufficiently divine off-hand what we ought to say, though I have a suspicion.” “You certainly, I presume,” said I,

chinese:
明白：歌曲由三样东西构成——歌词、曲调和节奏。”
“是的，”他说，“这点我明白。”
“而就歌词而言，它与未唱出来的言辞毫无区别，都必须符合我们规定的样式和方式，不是吗？”
“对。”他说。
“此外，曲调和节奏必须服从言辞。”
“当然。”
“但我们说过，我们的言辞中不需要哀歌和悲叹。”
“不需要。”
“那么，
english: “have sufficient a understanding of this—that the song is composed of three things, the words, the tune, and the rhythm?” “Yes,” said he, “that much.” “And so far as it is words, it surely in no manner differs from words not sung in the requirement of conformity to the patterns and manner that we have prescribed?” “True,” he said. “And again, the music and the rhythm must follow the speech.” “Of course.” “But we said we did not require dirges and lamentations in words.” “We do not.” “What, then,

chinese:
哪些调式具有哀歌的性质？告诉我，因为你懂音乐。”
“混合吕底亚调式，”他说，“还有紧张的、音高较高的吕底亚调式，以及类似的调式。”
“那么，”我说，“这些必须除去。因为，即使对那些应当力求成为最优秀的女人，它们也没有用，更不用说男人了。”
“当然。”
“再说，醉酒最不适合护卫者，柔弱和懒散也是如此。”
“是的。”
“那么，哪些是柔靡、适于饮宴的调式？”
“有一些伊奥尼亚调式，还有一些吕底亚调式，叫作松弛的调式。”
english: are the dirge-like modes of music? Tell me, for you are a musician.” “The mixed Lydian,” he said, “and the tense or higher Lydian, and similar modes.” “These, then,” said I, “we must do away with. For they are useless even to women who are to make the best of themselves, let alone to men.” “Assuredly.” “But again, drunkenness is a thing most unbefitting guardians, and so is softness and sloth.” “Yes.” “What, then, are the soft and convivial modes?” “There are certain Ionian and also Lydian modes that are called lax.”

chinese:
“你会给战士采用这些调式吗？”
“完全不会，”他说，“这样看来，你留下的就是多里亚调式和弗里吉亚调式了。”
“我不懂这些音乐调式，”我说，“但请给我们留下一种调式：它能够恰当地模仿勇敢的人在战争或其他被迫从事的事务中的言辞和声调；当他遭受挫败，无论是负伤、面临死亡，还是遭到其他不幸，
english: “Will you make any use of them for warriors?” “None at all,” he said; “but it would seem that you have left the Dorian and the Phrygian.” “I don’t know the musical modes,” I said, “but leave us that mode that would fittingly imitate the utterances and the accents of a brave man who is engaged in warfare or in any enforced business, and who, when he has failed, either meeting wounds or death or having fallen into some other mishap,

chinese: 在所有这些处境中，他都坚定地忍耐，面对命运，抵挡它的打击。再留下一种，适合这样的人从事和平的事务，不是出于强迫，而是自愿：他或是在劝说、恳求别人——对神用祈祷，对人用教导和规劝；或是反过来，顺从向他恳求、教导他或试图改变他意见的别人，因此如愿以偿，却不表现得傲慢，而是在这一切中保持谦逊和节制，
english: in all these conditions confronts fortune with steadfast endurance and repels her strokes. And another for such a man engaged in works of peace, not enforced but voluntary, either trying to persuade somebody of something and imploring him—whether it be a god, through prayer, or a man, by teaching and admonition—or contrariwise yielding himself to another who petitioning or teaching him or trying to change his opinions, and in consequence faring according to his wish, and not bearing himself arrogantly, but in all this acting modestly and moderately

chinese:
安然接受结果。请留下这两种调式——适于被迫和自愿处境的调式——它们最能模仿节制而勇敢的人在失败或成功时的言辞；留下这些吧。”
“那么，”他说，“你要我留下的，正是我刚才说的那些。”
“那么，”我说，“我们的歌曲和曲调就不需要许多弦的乐器，也不需要音域包罗所有调式的乐器。”
“我认为不需要。”他说。
“那么，我们也不会供养制作三角琴、竖琴，以及其他一切
english: and acquiescing in the outcome. Leave us these two modes—the forced and the voluntary—that will best imitate the utterances of men failing or succeeding, the temperate, the brave—leave us these.” “Well,” said he, “you are asking me to leave none other than those I just spoke of.” “Then,” said I, “we shall not need in our songs and airs instruments of many strings or whose compass includes all the harmonies.” “Not in my opinion,” said he. “Then we shall not maintain makers of triangles and harps and all other

chinese:
多弦、多调式乐器的人。”
“看来不会。”
“那么，你会允许制造管笛和吹奏管笛的人进入城邦吗？管笛难道不是乐器中最‘多弦’的，连那些能奏出一切调式的乐器本身，不也是在模仿它吗？”
“显然如此。”他说。
“这样，”我说，“你留下了里拉琴和基萨拉琴。这些在城邦里有用；在乡野，牧人则可以有一支小笛子吹奏。”
“我们的论证指向这个结论。”他说。
english: many stringed and poly-harmonic instruments.” “Apparently not.” “Well, will you admit to the city flute-makers and flute-players? Or is not the flute the most ‘many-stringed’ of instruments and do not the pan-harmonics themselves imitate it?” “Clearly,” he said. “You have left,” said I, “the lyre and the cither. These are useful in the city, and in the fields the shepherds would have a little piccolo to pipe on.” “So our argument indicates,” he said.

chinese:
“朋友，我们宁取阿波罗和阿波罗的乐器，不取马尔叙阿斯和他的乐器，并不是什么标新立异。”
“是的，凭上天起誓！”他说，“我想不是。”
“凭狗起誓，”我说，“我们不知不觉地，把不久前还说是放纵的那座城邦净化了。”
“这表明我们有理智。”他说。
“那么来吧，让我们把净化完成。调式之后，便应当考察节奏：我们不应追求基本节拍的复杂和繁多，而必须观察，哪些节奏属于有秩序而勇敢的生活；观察清楚之后，
english:
“We are not innovating, my friend, in preferring Apollo and the instruments of Apollo to Marsyas and his instruments.” “No, by heaven!” he said, “I think not.” “And by the dog,” said I, “we have all unawares purged the city which a little while ago we said was wanton.” “In that we show our good sense,” he said.

“Come then, let us complete the purification.”

For upon harmonies would follow the consideration of rhythms: we must not pursue complexity nor great variety in the basic movements, but must observe what are the rhythms of a life that is orderly and brave, and after observing them

chinese:
就要求音步和曲调去适应这种人的言辞，而不是让言辞去适应音步和曲调。这些节奏究竟是什么，应由你像刚才说明调式那样，告诉我们。”
“说真的，”他说，“我可说不出来。我确实注意到，也能够说出：音步大约由三种基本形式组合而成，正如声音有四种基本形式，由它们产生一切调式一样。但哪一种模仿哪一种生活，我就说不出来了。”
english: require the foot and the air to conform to that kind of man’s speech and not the speech to the foot and the tune. What those rhythms would be, it is for you to tell us as you did the musical modes.” “Nay, in faith,” he said, “I cannot tell. For that there are some three forms from which the feet are combined, just as there are four in the notes of the voice whence come all harmonies, is a thing that I have observed and could tell. But which are imitations of which sort of life, I am unable to say.”

chinese: “那么，”我说，“在这一点上，我们也要请教达蒙：哪些音步适合表现卑鄙、傲慢、疯狂或其他恶，哪些节奏应当留下来表现与之相反的品质。我记得听他含糊地谈起一种他叫作‘武装音步’的复合音步，还有扬抑抑格和英雄格；他把它们加以排列，我不知道具体怎样，使长短音交替时，上下两部分相等。如果我没有记错，他还用过‘抑扬格’这个名称，另有一种他叫作‘扬抑格’的音步，
english: “Well,” said I, “on this point we will take counsel with Damon, too, as to which are the feet appropriate to illiberality, and insolence or madness or other evils, and what rhythms we must leave for their opposites; and I believe I have heard him obscurely speaking of a foot that he called the enoplios, a composite foot, and a dactyl and an heroic foot, which he arranged, I know not how, to be equal up and down in the interchange of long and short, and unless I am mistaken he used the term iambic, and there was another foot that he called the trochaic,

chinese:
并加上长与短的音量。在其中一些音步上，我想，他不仅批评或赞许节奏本身，也同样批评或赞许音步的速度；也许他评的是二者的某种组合，我说不清。不过，正如我所说，这件事还是留待达蒙考察。要弄清这些事情的真相，得有一番不短的讨论。你有不同看法吗？”
“不，凭上天起誓，我没有。”
“但这一点你能够确定：姿态的美与丑，分别伴随着好的节奏与坏的节奏。”
“当然。”
“而且，
english: and he added the quantities long and short. And in some of these, I believe, he censured and commended the tempo of the foot no less than the rhythm itself, or else some combination of the two; I can’t say. But, as I said, let this matter be postponed for Damon’s consideration. For to determine the truth of these would require no little discourse. Do you think otherwise?” “No, by heaven, I do not.” “But this you are able to determine—that seemliness and unseemliness are attendant upon the good rhythm and the bad.” “Of course.” “And, further, that

chinese:
好的节奏伴随着美好的表达，并与之相适应；坏的节奏则伴随着相反的表达。和谐与不和谐也同样如此——如果正如我们刚才所说，是节奏和调式服从言辞，而不是言辞服从它们的话。”
“它们当然必须服从言辞。”他说。
“那么，表达的方式和言辞本身呢？”我说，“它们难道不是随灵魂的性情而来，并与之相适应吗？”
“当然。”
“其余的一切又都随着表达而来？”
“是的。”
“那么，言辞的美好、和声的美好、姿态的优雅，
english: good rhythm and bad rhythm accompany, the one fair diction, assimilating itself thereto, and the other the opposite, and so of the apt and the unapt, if, as we were just now saying, the rhythm and harmony follow the words and not the words these.” “They certainly must follow the speech,” he said. “And what of the manner of the diction, and the speech?” said I. “Do they not follow and conform to the disposition of the soul?” “Of course.” “And all the rest to the diction?” “Yes.” “Good speech, then, good accord, and good grace,

chinese:
以及节奏的美好，都随着良好的性情而来。这里说的不是我们委婉地称为‘心地好’的那种头脑软弱，而是品格和心智真正良好而美的性情。”
“完全如此。”他说。
“如果我们的年轻人要完成真正属于自己的工作，不就必须到处追求这些品质吗？”
“确实必须。”
“而这些品质在绘画
english:
and good rhythm wait upon good disposition, not that weakness of head which we euphemistically style goodness of heart, but the truly good and fair disposition of the character and the mind.” “By all means,” he said. “And must not our youth pursue these everywhere if they are to do what it is truly theirs to do?” “They must indeed.”

“And there is surely much of these qualities in painting

chinese:
和一切类似的技艺中，当然也大量存在：编织、刺绣、建筑，以及家用器物的制作，都充满了这些品质；动物和植物天生的形体也一样。因为，在所有这些事物中，都有优美或丑陋。丑陋、坏的节奏和不和谐，与不良的言辞和恶劣的性情相近；而相反的形式，则是相反性情——节制而良好的性情——的表征和近亲。”
“完全如此。”他说。
english: and in all similar craftsmanship—weaving is full of them and embroidery and architecture and likewise the manufacture of household furnishings and thereto the natural bodies of animals and plants as well. For in all these there is grace or gracelessness. And gracelessness and evil rhythm and disharmony are akin to evil speaking and the evil temper but the opposites are the symbols and the kin of the opposites, the sober and good disposition.” “Entirely so,” he said.

chinese: “那么，我们应当监督的难道只有诗人吗？只要求他们把良好品格的形象写进诗里，否则便不得在我们这里作诗，就够了吗？还是也必须留意其他工匠，禁止他们在生物的形象、建筑或其他任何技艺的产物中，表现邪恶的性情、放纵、卑鄙和丑陋；如果不能遵守，就不许他们在我们这里从事自己的技艺？这样，我们的护卫者便不会在恶的表征中长大，仿佛置身于
english: “Is it, then, only the poets that we must supervise and compel to embody in their poems the semblance of the good character or else not write poetry among us, or must we keep watch over the other craftsmen, and forbid them to represent the evil disposition, the licentious, the illiberal, the graceless, either in the likeness of living creatures or in buildings or in any other product of their art, on penalty, if unable to obey, of being forbidden to practise their art among us, that our guardians may not be bred among symbols of evil, as it were

chinese: 长满毒草的牧场，日复一日地从许多这样的东西上随意啃食，以至于一点点、不知不觉地在自己的灵魂中积累、堆起大量的恶。相反，我们必须寻找那些有幸天资优异、能够追寻真正的美与优雅的工匠，使年轻人仿佛生活在一片有益健康的地方，从周围的一切得到益处；美的作品所散发的影响，吹向他们的眼睛或耳朵，就像从健康的地方吹来的微风，把健康带到身边，
english: in a pasturage of poisonous herbs, lest grazing freely and cropping from many such day by day they little by little and all unawares accumulate and build up a huge mass of evil in their own souls. But we must look for those craftsmen who by the happy gift of nature are capable of following the trail of true beauty and grace, that our young men, dwelling as it were in a salubrious region, may receive benefit from all things about them, whence the influence that emanates from works of beauty may waft itself to eye or ear like a breeze that brings from wholesome places health,

chinese:
从幼年起，便潜移默化地引导他们与美好的理性相似、相亲、相和谐。”
“是的，”他说，“这无疑是对他们最好的教育。”
“格劳孔，”我说，“诗乐教育之所以最有力量，难道不正是由于这个缘故吗？因为节奏和和谐比任何东西都更能深入灵魂内部，最有力地把握住它，给它带来优雅；教育得当，就赋予它优雅，
english: and so from earliest childhood insensibly guide them to likeness, to friendship, to harmony with beautiful reason.” “Yes,” he said, “that would be far the best education for them.” “And is it not for this reason, Glaucon,” said I, “that education in music is most sovereign, because more than anything else rhythm and harmony find their way to the inmost soul and take strongest hold upon it, bringing with them and imparting grace, if one is rightly trained,

chinese: 否则，就造成相反的结果。此外，一个接受过良好诗乐教育的人，对于制作不良或生长不良的事物中的缺陷和美的欠缺，能够最敏锐地察觉；他由此产生恰当的厌恶，会赞美美的事物，以之为乐，把它们接纳进自己的灵魂，滋养它的成长，使自己也成为美而善的人。
english:
and otherwise the contrary?”

And further, because omissions and the failure of beauty in things badly made or grown would be most quickly perceived by one who was properly educated in music, and so, feeling distaste rightly, he would praise beautiful things and take delight in them and receive them into his soul to foster its growth and become himself beautiful and good.

chinese:
对于丑的东西，他在还年幼、尚不能理解理由时，就会正确地加以反对和憎恶；而当理性到来，受过这种培养的人就会最先欢迎它，因为彼此相近，他能够认出它。”
“我的确认为，”他说，“这就是诗乐教育的根据。”
“那么，”我说，“这就像我们学习字母时一样：只有当那为数不多的字母，无论出现在哪种组合里，都不会逃过我们的辨认，我们才觉得自己学得够了；我们不因字母出现的地方
english: The ugly he would rightly disapprove of and hate while still young and yet unable to apprehend the reason, but when reason came the man thus nurtured would be the first to give her welcome, for by this affinity he would know her.” “I certainly think,” he said, “that such is the cause of education in music.” “It is, then,” said I, “as it was when we learned our letters and felt that we knew them sufficiently only when the separate letters did not elude us, appearing as few elements in all the combinations that convey them, and when we did not disregard them

chinese:
或小或大，就忽略它们，以为不必认出，而是急于在任何地方都分辨清楚，因为我们相信，做不到这一点，就永远不能算识字，也不能算熟练掌握字母。”
“对。”
“同样，如果水中或镜子里映出了字母的影像，在认识字母本身之前，我们也绝不可能认出它们；而这种认识属于同一种技艺和学习，不是吗？”
“完全如此。”
“那么，凭上天起誓，依同一道理，我说得难道不对吗：我们也永远不能成为真正懂诗乐的人——
english: in small things or great and think it unnecessary to recognize them, but were eager to distinguish them everywhere, in the belief that we should never be literate and letter-perfect till we could do this.” “True.” “And is it not also true that if there are any likenesses of letters reflected in water or mirrors, we shall never know them until we know the originals, but such knowledge belongs to the same art and discipline?” “By all means.” “Then, by heaven, am I not right in saying that by the same token we shall never be true musicians, either—

chinese:
无论是我们，还是我们着手培养的护卫者——除非我们能够在包含、呈现这些品质的一切组合中，辨认出节制、勇敢、慷慨、高尚，以及一切与它们相近的品质和它们的反面，并且无论这些品质及其形象出现在哪里，都能认出；不因事情琐细或重大而有所忽略，而相信对它们的认识属于同一种技艺和学习。”
“这个结论不可避免。”他说。
english: neither we nor the guardians that we have undertaken to educate—until we are able to recognize the forms of soberness, courage, liberality, and high-mindedness and all their kindred and their opposites, too, in all the combinations that contain and convey them, and to apprehend them and their images wherever found, disregarding them neither in trifles nor in great things, but believing the knowledge of them to belong to the same art and discipline?” “The conclusion is inevitable,” he said.

chinese:
“那么，”我说，“如果一个人灵魂中美好的性情，与身体形态上相应、协调而同类的美恰好结合在一起，对于能够欣赏的人来说，这难道不是最美的景象吗？”
“远比其他景象都美。”
“而最美的，当然也是最值得爱的。”
“当然。”
“那么，真正懂诗乐的人，会特别爱这样的人；如果有不协调之处，他就不会爱。”
“是的，”他说，“如果缺陷在灵魂上，他不会爱；但若缺陷在身体上，他会容忍，仍然愿意给予他的爱。”
english: “Then,” said I, “when there is a coincidence of a beautiful disposition in the soul and corresponding and harmonious beauties of the same type in the bodily form—is not this the fairest spectacle for one who is capable of its contemplation?” “Far the fairest.” “And surely the fairest is the most lovable.” “Of course.” “The true musician, then, would love by preference persons of this sort; but if there were disharmony he would not love this.” “No,” he said, “not if there was a defect in the soul; but if it were in the body he would bear with it and still be willing to bestow his love.”

chinese:
“我明白，”我说，“你现在或从前有过这样的爱人；我接受你的区分。不过请告诉我：节制与过度的快乐之间，能有什么相通之处吗？”
“怎么会有呢？”他说，“这种快乐和痛苦一样，都会使人失去自持。”
english: “I understand,” I said, “that you have or have had favorites of this sort and I grant your distinction. But tell me this—can there be any communion between soberness and extravagant pleasure?” “How could there be,” he said, “since such pleasure puts a man beside himself no less than pain?”

chinese:
“或者说，它与一般的德性之间，能有什么相通之处吗？”
“绝对没有。”
“但这种快乐与傲慢和放纵之间，有相通之处吗？”
“当然有。”
“你知道有什么快乐，比与阿佛洛狄忒相关的快乐更大、更强烈吗？”
“我不知道，”他说，“也不知道有比它更疯狂的快乐。”
“但是，正当的爱，不是以节制而和谐的方式，爱那有秩序而美的事物吗？”
“确实如此。”他说。
“那么，任何疯狂的东西，任何近于放纵的东西，都不得接近正当的爱？”
“不得接近。”
“那么，这一种快乐
english:
“Or between it and virtue generally?”

“By no means.” “But is there between pleasure and insolence and licence?” “Most assuredly.” “Do you know of greater or keener pleasure than that associated with Aphrodite?” “I don’t,” he said, “nor yet of any more insane.” “But is not the right love a sober and harmonious love of the orderly and the beautiful?” “It is indeed,” said he. “Then nothing of madness, nothing akin to licence, must be allowed to come nigh the right love?” “No.” “Then this kind of pleasure

chinese:
也不得接近它；正当地爱与被爱的爱者和被爱者，也不得与这种快乐有任何关系？”
“是的，凭上天起誓，苏格拉底，”他说，“它不得接近他们。”
“那么看来，你会在我们正在建立的城邦中这样立法：爱者如果能说服被爱者，可以为了高尚的目的，像父亲对儿子那样亲吻他、与他共处、抚触他；但除此以外，他与自己关爱的人相处，必须使人永远不会怀疑还有更进一步的事情，
english: may not come nigh, nor may lover and beloved who rightly love and are loved have anything to do with it?” “No, by heaven, Socrates,” he said, “it must not come nigh them.” “Thus, then, as it seems, you will lay down the law in the city that we are founding, that the lover may kiss and pass the time with and touch the beloved as a father would a son, for honorable ends, if he persuade him. But otherwise he must so associate with the objects of his care that there should never be any suspicion of anything further,

chinese:
否则就要被指责为缺乏品位和真正的诗乐教养。”
“正是如此。”他说。
“那么，你是否同意，我们关于诗乐的讨论已经到了终点？这个收尾当然合宜，因为教养的目的和完成，应当就是爱美。”
“我同意。”他说。
“在诗乐之后，我们的年轻人应当接受体育教育？”
“当然。”
“在这方面，他们也必须受到细心的训练，
english:
on penalty of being stigmatized for want of taste and true musical culture.” “Even so,” he said. “Do you not agree, then, that our discourse on music has come to an end? It has certainly made a fitting end, for surely the end and consummation of culture be love of the beautiful.” “I concur,” he said.

“After music our youth are to be educated by gymnastics?” “Certainly.” “In this too they must be carefully trained

chinese:
从童年一直贯穿终身。我相信方式应当如下，不过你也来考虑一下。就我而言，我不相信健全的身体凭自身的优良就能使灵魂变好；恰恰相反，良好的灵魂凭它的德性，能够使身体达到尽可能好的状态。你的意见如何？”
“我也这样认为。”
“那么，如果我们充分训练心智，把照料身体的细节交给它，
english: from boyhood through life, and the way of it is this, I believe; but consider it yourself too. For I, for my part, do not believe that a sound body by its excellence makes the soul good, but on the contrary that a good soul by its virtue renders the body the best that is possible. What is your opinion?” “I think so too.” “Then if we should sufficiently train the mind and turn over to it the minutiae of the care of the body,

chinese:
而我们只满足于指出准则或样式，不作冗长的叙说，这样做就是对的？”
“完全对。”
“我们说过，他们必须避免醉酒。因为在所有人中，最不能获准喝醉、连自己究竟在哪里都不知道的，就是护卫者。”
“是的，”他说，“护卫者竟然还需要别人护卫，实在荒唐。”
“接下来，他们的饮食怎样？这些人是在最大的竞赛中参赛的运动员，不是吗？”
“是的。”
“那么，我们身边所见那些运动员的身体状态，适合他们吗？”
english:
and content ourselves with merely indicating the norms or patterns, not to make a long story of it, we should acting rightly?” “By all means.” “From intoxication we said that they must abstain. For a guardian is surely the last person in the world to whom it is allowable to get drunk and not know where on earth he is.” “Yes,” he said, “it would absurd that a guardian should need a guard.” “What next about their food? These men are athletes in the greatest of contests, are they not?” “Yes.”

“Is, then, the bodily habit of the athletes we see about us suitable for such?”

chinese:
“也许适合。”
“不，”我说，“那是一种嗜睡的状态，而且健康很不稳固。你难道没有看到，他们把一生都睡过去了；只要稍稍偏离规定的生活制度，这些运动员就容易患上严重而急剧的疾病吗？”
“我看到了。”
“那么，”我说，“对于我们这些战争中的运动员，就需要一种更周到的训练方式：他们必须像不眠的猎犬，拥有尽可能敏锐的视觉和听觉；在行军作战中，饮水、食物常常改变，
english: “Perhaps.” “Nay,” said I, “that is a drowsy habit and precarious for health. Don’t you observe that they sleep away their lives, and that if they depart ever so little from their prescribed regimen these athletes are liable to great and violent diseases?” “I do.” “Then,” said I, “we need some more ingenious form of training for our athletes of war, since these must be as it were sleepless hounds, and have the keenest possible perceptions of sight and hearing, and in their campaigns undergo many changes

chinese:
又经常遭受烈日与风暴，健康却不能因此受到扰乱。”
“我也这样认为。”
“那么，最好的体育，不应当与我们刚才描绘的诗乐相近吗？”
“你是什么意思？”
“它应当是一种简朴而灵活的体育，尤其适于战争训练。”
“怎样做到呢？”
“这一点，”我说，“甚至可以向荷马学习。因为你知道，他描写出征英雄的宴饮时，并没有
english: in their drinking water, their food, and in exposure to the heat of the sun and to storms, without disturbance of their health.” “I think so.” “Would not, then, the best gymnastics be akin to the music that we were just now describing?” “What do you mean?” “It would be a simple and flexible gymnastic, and especially so in the training for war.” “In what way?” “One could learn that,” said I, “even from Homer. For you are aware that in the banqueting of the heroes on campaign he does not

chinese:
让他们吃鱼，也没有给他们煮肉，只给烤肉；这是士兵最容易弄到的。因为可以说，无论到哪里，直接用火，总比带着锅碗更容易张罗。”
“确实如此。”
“而且，据我所知，荷马从来没有提到甜食。所有接受训练的人不都明白这一点吗：若要保持身体的良好状态，就必须完全不吃这类东西。”
“他们知道这一点，又确实不吃，
english: feast them on fish, nor on boiled meat, but only on roast, which is what soldiers could most easily procure. For everywhere, one may say, it is of easier provision to use the bare fire than to convey pots and pans along.” “Indeed it is.” “Neither, as I believe, does Homer ever make mention of sweet meats. Is not that something which all men in training understand—that if one is to keep his body in good condition he must abstain from such things altogether?” “They are right,”

chinese:
是做得对的。”他说。
“那么，朋友，如果你认为这条路是对的，你显然不会赞成叙拉古人的餐桌，也不会赞成西西里那些花样繁多的菜肴。”
“我想不会。”
“那么，你也会反对那些应当保持良好体魄的人，找一个科林斯姑娘做情妇？”
“当然反对。”
“也反对阿提卡糕点那些看似诱人的美味？”
“必定如此。”
“大体说来，我想，若把这样的食物和生活方式，比作采用全部调式、
english: he said, “in that they know it and do abstain.” “Then, my friend, if you think this is the right way, you apparently do not approve of a Syracusan table and Sicilian variety of made dishes.” “I think not.” “You would frown, then, on a little Corinthian maid as the chère amie of men who were to keep themselves fit?” “Most certainly.” “And also on the seeming delights of Attic pastry?” “Inevitably.” “In general, I take it, if we likened that kind of food and regimen to music and song expressed in the pan-harmonic mode and

chinese:
使用各种节奏的音乐和歌曲，这个比较应当恰当。”
“正是如此。”
“在诗乐中，繁多变化生出放纵；在饮食中，则生出疾病，不是吗？而诗乐中的简朴，使灵魂产生节制；体育训练中的简朴，使身体产生健康。”
“完全正确。”他说。
“当放纵
english:
in every variety of rhythm it would be a fair comparison.” “Quite so.” “And here variety engendered licentiousness, did it not, but here disease? While simplicity in music begets sobriety in the souls, and in gymnastic training it begets health in bodies.” “Most true,” he said.

“And when licentiousness

chinese:
和疾病在城邦中增多，不就会开设许多法庭和诊所吗？诉讼诡辩的技艺和医术，也会趾高气扬，因为连许多自由人都对它们极其认真。”
“怎么会不这样呢？”他说。
“一个城邦不仅卑下的体力劳动者需要高明的医生和法官，就连自称受过自由人式教育的人也需要他们；还有比这更确凿的证据，说明这座城邦的教育恶劣而可耻吗？你难道不认为，
english:
and disease multiply in a city, are not many courts of law and dispensaries opened, and the arts of chicane and medicine give themselves airs when even free men in great numbers take them very seriously?” “How can they help it?” he said.

“Will you be able to find a surer proof of an evil and shameful state of education in a city than the necessity of first-rate physicians and judges, not only for the base and mechanical, but for those who claim to have been bred in the fashion of free men? Do you not think

chinese:
一个人由于自己缺少正义，竟须从别人那里借用正义，使那些人成为自己的主人和裁判，这是可耻的，是教养不良的显著标志吗？”
“这是世上最可耻的事情。”
“是吗？”我说，“还是下面这种更可耻：一个人不仅把一生最好的时光耗在法庭上，不是作被告，就是作原告；而且因为完全没有真正的价值判断，竟然以此自夸，以为自己是个聪明人，能够把不正义的行为蒙混过去，
english: it disgraceful and a notable mark of bad breeding to have to make use of a justice imported from others, who thus become your masters and judges, from lack of such qualities in yourself?” “The most shameful thing in the world.” “Is it?” said I, “or is this still more shameful—when a man only wears out the better part of his days in the courts of law as defendant or accuser, but from the lack of all true sense of values is led to plume himself on this very thing, as being a smart fellow to ‘put over’ an unjust act

chinese:
巧妙地使出一切花招和手段，想尽一切逃避的办法，从每一种束缚中挣脱，以便挫败正义；而做这一切，为的只是琐碎、没有价值的东西，因为他不知道，把自己的生活安排得无须依赖一个打瞌睡的陪审员，是何等更加高尚、更加美好的事。”
“这一种，”他说，“比前一种还可耻。”
“还有，”我说，“一个人需要医术，不只是因为受伤，或偶然患上某种时令病，
english: and cunningly to try every dodge and practice, every evasion, and wriggle out of every hold in defeating justice, and that too for trifles and worthless things, because he does not know how much nobler and better it is to arrange his life so as to have no need of a nodding juryman?” “That is,” said he, “still more shameful than the other.” “And to require medicine,” said I, “not merely for wounds or the incidence of some seasonal maladies,

chinese:
而是由于懒惰和我们所说的那种生活方式，把身体弄得像沼泽一样，充满气胀和体液，逼得那些聪明的阿斯克勒庇俄斯后裔，为疾病发明‘流泻’、‘胀气’之类的名称——你不觉得这可耻吗？”
“这些疾病的名称，”他说，“确实是新奇而怪异得很。”
“我想，”我说，“在阿斯克勒庇俄斯的时代，并没有这一类东西。我的推断来自这件事：在特洛伊，他的儿子们
english: but, because of sloth and such a regimen as we described, to fill one’s body up with winds and humors like a marsh and compel the ingenious sons of Aesculapius to invent for diseases such names as fluxes and flatulences—don’t you think that disgraceful?” “Those surely are,” he said, “new-fangled and monstrous strange names of diseases.” “There was nothing of the kind, I fancy,” said I, “in the days of Aesculapius. I infer this from the fact that at Troy his sons

chinese: 并没有责怪那位姑娘；她给受伤的欧律皮洛斯喝了一碗普拉姆诺斯酒调成的饮料，里面撒了许多大麦粉和磨碎的乳酪——
english: did not find fault with the damsel who gave to the wounded Eurypylus to drink a posset of Pramnian wine plentifully sprinkled with barley and gratings of cheese,

chinese:
这些肯定是容易引发炎症的配料——他们也没有责备负责照料伤者的帕特罗克洛斯。”
“对那种状况的人来说，”他说，“这确实是一种奇怪的饮料。”
“并不奇怪，”我说，“只要你想到，在赫罗狄科斯之前，从前那些阿斯克勒庇俄斯的传人，并不用我们今天这种娇养疾病的疗法。赫罗狄科斯原本是一位体育教练，后来体弱多病，便把
english:
inflammatory ingredients of a surety, nor did they censure Patroclus, who was in charge of the case.”

“It was indeed,” said he, “a strange potion for a man in that condition.” “Not strange,” said I, “if you reflect that the former Asclepiads made no use of our modern coddling medication of diseases before the time of Herodicus. But Herodicus was a trainer and became a valetudinarian, and blended

chinese:
体育和医术混合起来，首先、也最厉害地折磨了他自己，接着又折磨了许多后来的人。”
“怎么回事？”他说。
“就是把自己的死拖得很长，”我说，“因为他的疾病不能治愈，他终日看守着它，却无法治好；他一天天活着，不能承担生活的事务，只要稍稍偏离固定的生活制度，就遭受如同地狱般的折磨。他凭自己的医术与死亡抗争，终于赢得的奖品，是一个昏聩的晚年。”
“他的医术赢来的奖品，真是高贵啊。”他说。
english: gymnastics and medicine, for the torment first and chiefly of himself and then of many successors.” “How so?” he said. “By lingering out his death,” said I; “for living in perpetual observance of his malady, which was incurable, he was not able to effect a cure, but lived through his days unfit for the business of life, suffering the tortures of the damned if he departed a whit from his fixed regimen, and struggling against death by reason of his science he won the prize of a doting old age.” “A noble prize indeed for his science,” he said.

chinese:
“对这样的人来说，倒很相称，”我说，“因为他不知道：阿斯克勒庇俄斯不把这种医术传给后代，并非出于无知，也并非不熟悉它，而是因为他知道，在所有治理良好的社会里，城邦中的每个人都有一份必须完成的工作，谁也没有闲暇一辈子生病、一辈子给自己治病。奇怪的是，对于工匠，我们明白这一点；对于富人和那些所谓幸运的人，却看不见了。”
“怎么说？”他问。
english: “The appropriate one,” said I, “for a man who did not know that it was not from ignorance or inacquaintance with this type of medicine that Aesculapius did not discover it to his descendants, but because he knew that for all well-governed peoples there is a work assigned to each man in the city which he must perform, and no one has leisure to be sick and doctor himself all his days. And this we absurdly enough perceive in the case of a craftsman, but don’t see in the case of the rich and so-called fortunate.” “How so?” he said.

chinese: “一个木匠，”我说，“生病时，希望医生给他一种药，用催吐把病排出去，或用泻药、烧灼、刀割除掉疾病。但如果有人为他开出长期疗养的方子，要他把头包起来，再加上其他一套措施，他就赶忙说，自己没有闲暇生病；这种整日挂念疾病、把眼前工作放在一边的生活，不值得过。于是，他告别这种医生，
english: “A carpenter,” said I, “when he is sick expects his physician to give him a drug which will operate as an emetic on the disease, or to get rid of it by purging or the use of cautery or the knife. But if anyone prescribes for him a long course of treatment with swathings about the head and their accompaniments, he hastily says that he has no leisure to be sick and that such a life of preoccupation with his illess and neglect of the work that lies before him isn’t worth living. And thereupon he bids farewell to that kind of physician,

chinese:
回到惯常的生活方式，恢复健康，活着办理自己的事务；或者，如果身体承受不了，他就死去，从此摆脱全部烦恼。”
“对于这样的人，”他说，“这看来就是医术的正确用法。”
“原因难道不是，”我说，
english:
enters upon his customary way of life, regains his health, and lives attending to his affairs—or, if his body is not equal to strain, he dies and is freed from all his troubles.” “For such a man,” he said, “that appears to be the right use of medicine.”

“And is not the reason,” I said,

chinese:
“他有一份工作，而若以不能做自己的工作为条件，生命就不值得接受吗？”
“显然是的。”他说。
“但我们说，富人并没有这样一份指定的工作，使他一旦不得不放弃，生活就难以忍受。”
“我没听说他有。”
“怎么，你没有听过福库利得斯的那句话吗？一个人‘积起财富’以后，就应当修习德性。”
“我想，在这以前也该如此。”他说。
“这一点我们先不与他争论，”我说，“且弄清楚：这种德性是不是富人必须践行的，
english: “that he had a task and that life wasn’t worth acceptance on condition of not doing his work?” “Obviously,” he said. “But the rich man, we say, has no such appointed task, the necessity of abstaining from which renders life intolerable.” “I haven’t heard of any.” “Why, haven’t you heard that saying of Phocylides, that after a man has ‘made his pile’ he ought to practice virtue?” “Before, too, I fancy,” he said. “Let us not quarrel with him on that point,” I said, “but inform ourselves whether this virtue is something for the rich man to practise,

chinese:
若不践行，生活便不可忍受；还是我们要以为，终日养病虽然妨碍专心从事木工和其他技艺，却不妨碍履行福库利得斯的劝告。”
“的确，”他说，“这种超出单纯体育范围的、对身体的过度照料，是最大的障碍。它妨碍家务，妨碍服兵役，也妨碍在城邦里担任坐着办公的职务。”
“而最主要的是，它给一切学习、思考和独自沉思设置困难，
english: and life is intolerable if he does not, or whether we are to suppose that while valetudinarianism is a hindrance to single-minded attention to carpentry and the other arts, it is no obstacle to the fulfilment of Phocylides’ exhortation.” “Yes, indeed,” he said, “this excessive care for the body that goes beyond simple gymnastics is the greatest of all obstacles. For it is troublesome in household affairs and military service and sedentary offices in the city.” “And, chief of all, it puts difficulties in the way of any kind of instruction, thinking, or private meditation,

chinese:
总是想象自己头痛、眩晕，把这些毛病归因于哲学。因此，在任何需要践行、检验这种德性的地方，它都处处妨碍。因为它使人总以为自己有病，永远为自己的身体焦虑不安。”
“自然如此。”他说。
“那么，我们不该说，阿斯克勒庇俄斯正因为知道这一点，才对那些由于天性和生活方式而身体健全，

like a beast by violence and savagery, and in his brute ignorance and ineptitude lives a life of disharmony and gracelessness.” “That is entirely true,” he said.

“农夫中最优秀的人，不就是最会务农的人吗？”
“是的。”
“在这里，既然我们希望统治者是护卫者中最优秀的人，他们不就必须是最好的护卫者，最关心城邦的人吗？”
“是的。”
“那么，他们首先必须对这些事务有理解力、有能力，
